Under Section-130, the magistrate must issue a written order explaining the basis for the proceedings, the proposed bond amount, its duration and the number of sureties required. A peace bond can be required for up to one year, and the amount must not be excessive. The person must be given an opportunity to explain why they should not be required to furnish the bond. The magistrate then conducts an inquiry under Section-135. Separately, Section-163 allows an executive magistrate to issue urgent orders to prevent specified dangers or disturbances, including restricting public gatherings when legal conditions are met. Detention is not automatic once proceedings begin. Under Section-135(3), an SEM may require immediate security if necessary to prevent a breach of peace or danger to public safety. If the person fails to furnish it, they may be detained until the inquiry concludes. Under Section-136, the magistrate can order security if the inquiry establishes it is necessary. Under Section-137, the person must be discharged if the need for security isn’t established. Failure to furnish security: Section-141 provides for imprisonment in specified circumstances, including failure to furnish security after a final order or breach of a qualifying bond. A surety undertakes responsibility under a bond to help ensure the person concerned meets its conditions. Under Section-140, an SEM can reject a surety found unfit, but must conduct an inquiry, give the parties a reasonable opportunity to be heard and record reasons in writing. The first surety’s photograph on the bond allegedly didn’t match his Aadhaar. He reportedly failed to produce another valid ID and gave unsatisfactory answers during questioning. The SEM concluded the sureties didn’t have sufficient control over the activists to ensure their presence when required. The inquiry under Section-135 is conducted like the trial of a summons case, and it must be completed within six months, failing which the proceedings end unless the magistrate records special reasons. A bond for keeping the peace, if ordered, may be forfeited if its conditions are breached. A person aggrieved by an order requiring security, or by the rejection of a surety, can appeal to the Court of Session. Article 22(2) of the Constitution and Section-58 of the BNSS require that anyone arrested be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.

title: Test #21: The Ahom Kingdom - Centuries of Endurance
text: The Ahom kingdom of Assam maintained its political independence for almost six-centuries (1228-1826) and successfully resisted several invasions and attempts at annexation. The military strategy of the Ahoms relied on exploiting the local terrain rather than engaging in direct confrontation. Ahom commanders possessed detailed knowledge of Assam’s forests, river systems, and monsoon cycles, which invading forces generally lacked. A decisive check on Mughal ambitions in the region came in 1671, when the Ahom commander Lachit Borphukan and his 10,000 men defeated a Mughal fleet of 30,000 soldiers at the Battle of Saraighat, securing the Brahmaputra effective territorial boundary. Despite repeated attempts by the Mughals to annex the Brahmaputra valley, the Ahoms successfully defended their territories against Mughal invasion. The first Ahom-Mughal clash took place in 1615 near Samdhara. Mughal forces under Abu Bakr made early gains but were soon compelled to retreat. By 1616, the Ahoms had recovered the lost territory, setting a pattern that would recur over the next sixty years. In 1662, Mir Jumla captured the Ahom capital, Garhgaon. Subsequently, a treaty was imposed on King Jayadhvaj Singha. However, the king defied the Mughals and renounced the treaty within a year of the Mughal withdrawal, and the Ahoms retained their independence. The Ahoms’ successful resistance against the might of the Mughal empire is a remarkable story of bravery, pride, and endurance. Ahom endurance rested on a combination of strategic alliance-building, guerrilla tactics, Assam’s challenging geography, and the Paik system of military-administrative organisation. The Ahom navy also played a key role, using light, fast boats, called bachari, built specifically for river warfare, which gave them an advantage over Mughal fleets. In the 13th century, the Ahom ethnic group migrated from present-day Myanmar to the Brahmaputra Valley and formed the Ahom kingdom there. During both the Sultanate and the Mughal periods, the Ahom rulers offered stiff resistance to attempts at expansion into the Northeast. Their unique paik system called on every able-bodied man to provide service to the state through labour or military duty in exchange for land rights. This allowed the rulers to create public infrastructure and maintain a large standing force without a permanent army. Over time, the Ahoms assimilated the local culture, promoted agriculture, encouraged diverse faiths, and contributed to the rich traditions of Assam. In the 17th century, when Aurangzeb sent Mughal forces, briefly capturing the Ahom capital Garhgaon, the Ahoms used their knowledge of the terrain dense forests, hills and rivers and persistent guerrilla tactics to repulse the attack, although the latter had more men and a larger fleet of river boats. Ultimately, the Ahom were able to preserve their independence. Ram Singh, the general of the Mughal army, praised the Ahom warriors in these terms: “Every Assamese soldier is expert in rowing boats, in shooting arrows, in digging trenches, and in wielding guns and cannons. I have not seen such specimens of versatility in any other part of India.” The decline of the Ahom kingdom began only in the early 19th century, when internal rivalries among the nobility weakened the state. The Moamoria rebellion of the late eighteenth century had already strained the paik system and disturbed agricultural production. Repeated Burmese invasions then reduced royal authority further, and the British entered Assam in 1824 during the First Anglo-Burmese War. By the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826, the Burmese withdrew, and Assam passed under British control. Even so, the Ahom legacy of resilience, cultural harmony, and the courage of its warriors continues to inspire people across the entire region today.

title: Test #22: The Inteview - By Christopher Silvester
text: Since its invention a little over 130 years ago, the interview has become a commonplace of journalism. Today, almost everybody who is literate will have read an interview at some point in their lives, while from the other point of view, several thousand celebrities have been interviewed over the years, some of them repeatedly. So it is hardly surprising that opinions of the interview of its functions, methods and merits vary considerably. Some might make quite extravagant claims for it as being, in its highest form, a source of truth, and, in its practice, an art. Others, usually celebrities who see themselves as its victims, might despise the interview as an unwarranted intrusion into their lives, or feel that it somehow diminishes them, just as in some primitive cultures it is believed that if one takes a photographic portrait of somebody then one is stealing that person’s soul. V. S. Naipaul1 ‘feels that some people are wounded by interviews and lose a part of themselves,’ Lewis Carroll, the creator of Alice in Wonderland, was said to have had ‘a just horror of the interviewer’ and he never consented to be interviewed It was his horror of being lionized which made him thus repel would be acquaintances, interviewers, and the persistent petitioners for his autograph and he would afterwards relate the stories of his success in silencing all such people with much satisfaction and amusement. Rudyard Kipling expressed an even more condemnatory attitude towards the interviewer. His wife, Caroline, writes in her diary for 14 October 1892 that their day was ‘wrecked by two reporters from Boston’. She reports her husband as saying to the reporters, “Why do I refuse to be interviewed? Because it is immoral! It is a crime, just as much of a crime as an offence against my person, as an assault, and just as much merits punishment. It is cowardly and vile. No respectable man would ask it, much less give it,” Yet Kipling had himself perpetrated such an ‘assault’ on Mark Twain only a few years before. H. G. Well in an interview in 1894 referred to ‘the interviewing ordeal’, but was a fairly frequent interviewee and forty years later found himself interviewing Joseph Stalin4. Saul Bellow5, who has consented to be interviewed on several occasions, nevertheless once described interviews as being like thumbprints on his windpipe. Yet despite the drawbacks of the interview, it is a supremely serviceable medium of communication. “These days, more than at any other time, our most vivid impressions of our contemporaries are through interviews,” Denis Brian has written. “Almost everything of moment reaches us through one man asking questions of another. Because of this, the interviewer holds a position of unprecedented power and influence.” Journalists are puzzled. And sometimes publishers. And this is because journalists and publishers believe that people like trash and don’t like difficult reading experiences. Consider there are six billion people on this planet. The Name of the Rose sold between 10 and 15 million copies. So in a way I reached only a small percentage of readers. But it is exactly these kinds of readers who don’t want easy experiences. Or at least don’t always want this. I myself, at 9 pm after dinner, watch television and want to see either ‘Miami Vice’ or ‘Emergency Room’. I enjoy it and I need it. But not all day. That’s possible. But let me tell you another story, because I often tell stories like a Chinese wise man. My American publisher said while she loved my book, she didn’t expect to sell more than 3,000 copies in a country where nobody has seen a cathedral or studies Latin. So I was given an advance for 3,000 copies, but in the end it sold two or three million in the U.S. A lot of books have been written about the medieval past far before mine. I think the success of the book is a mystery. Nobody can predict it. I think if I had written The Name of the Rose ten years earlier or ten years later, it wouldn’t have been the same.

title: Test #23: Poets and Pancakes
text: Pancake was the brand name of the make-up material that Gemini Studios bought in truck-loads. Greta Garbo must have used it, Miss Gohar must have used it, Vyjayantimala must also have used it but Rati Agnihotri may not have even heard of it. The make-up department of the Gemini Studios was in the upstairs of a building that was believed to have been Robert Clive’s stables. A dozen other buildings in the city are said to have been his residence. For his brief life and an even briefer stay in Madras, Robert Clive seems to have done a lot of moving, besides fighting some impossible battles in remote corners of India and marrying a maiden in St. Mary’s Church in Fort St. George in Madras. The make-up room had the look of a hair-cutting salon with lights at all angles around half a dozen large mirrors. They were all incandescent lights, so you can imagine the fiery misery of those subjected to make-up. The make-up department was first headed by a Bengali who became too big for a studio and left. He was succeeded by a Maharashtrian who was assisted by a Dharwar Kannadiga, an Andhra, a Madras Indian Christian, an Anglo-Burmese and the usual local Tamils. All this shows that there was a great deal of national integration long before A.I.R. and Doordarshan began broadcasting programmes on national integration. This gang of nationally integrated make-up men could turn any decent-looking person into a hideous crimson hued monster with the help of truckloads of pancake and a number of other locally made potions and lotions. Those were the days of mainly indoor shooting, and only five per cent of the film was shot outdoors. I suppose the sets and studio lights needed the girls and boys to be made to look ugly in order to look presentable in the movie. A strict hierarchy was maintained in the make-up department. The chief make-up man made the chief actors and actresses ugly, his senior assistant the ‘second’ hero and heroine, the junior assistant the main comedian, and so forth. The players who played the crowd were the responsibility of the office boy. (Even the make-up department of the Gemini Studio had an ‘office boy’!) On the days when there was a crowd-shooting, you could see him mixing his paint in a giant vessel and slapping it on the crowd players. The idea was to close every pore on the surface of the face in the process of applying make-up. He wasn’t exactly a ‘boy’; he was in his early forties, having entered the studios years ago in the hope of becoming a star actor or a top screen writer, director or lyrics writer. He was a bit of a poet. In those days I worked in a cubicle, two whole sides of which were French windows. (I didn’t know at that time they were called French windows.) Seeing me sitting at my desk tearing up newspapers day in and day out, most people thought I was doing next to nothing. It is likely that the Boss thought likewise too. So anyone who felt I should be given some occupation would barge into my cubicle and deliver an extended lecture. The ‘boy’ in the make-up department had decided I should be enlightened on how great literary talent was being allowed to go waste in a department fit only for barbers and perverts. Soon I was praying for crowd-shooting all the time. Nothing short of it could save me from his epics. In all instances of frustration, you will always find the anger directed towards a single person openly or covertly and this man of the make-up department was convinced that all his woes, ignominy and neglect were due to Kothamangalam Subbu. Subbu was the No. 2 at Gemini Studios. He couldn’t have had a more encouraging opening in films than our grown-up make-up boy had. On the contrary he must have had to face more uncertain and difficult times, for when he began his career, there were no firmly established film producing companies or studios. Even in the matter of education, specially formal education, Subbu couldn’t have had an appreciable lead over our boy. But by virtue of being born a Brahmin a virtue, indeed! he must have had exposure to more affluent situations and people.

title: Test #24: Successful Adoption of Agrivoltaic in Farming
text: Agrivoltaics, or AgriPV, offers an opportunity to take that purpose forward by enabling farmers to produce clean electricity while continuing to cultivate their land. The successful efforts of the Government of India in the form of PM-KUSUM are already evident in the solarisation of irrigation. Further efforts are being made to accelerate the generation of solar energy through creation of separate space for AgriPV under the next phase of PM-KUSUM. From October 21-23, India will host the 7th-AgriVoltaics World Conference at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi. Its theme, ‘Powering the Global South’, speaks directly to the responsibility India is ready to shoulder. We want the benefits of agricultural innovation and the energy transition to reach the small and marginal farmers who constitute about 86% of India’s farmers. The Agrivoltaic designs should generally aim to maintain around 70% or more of natural incoming radiation at the crop canopy, while adjustable PV panels can provide additional flexibility during radiation-sensitive growth stages. Agrivoltaics combines cultivation and solar generation on the same land through structures and spacing suited to farming. It can give the cultivator an additional source of revenue from electricity. Where solar energy replaces diesel or purchased power, it can also reduce costs. The favourable microclimate under AgriPV provides additional protection against heat stress, drought, excessive solar radiation, and hail. Domestic manufacturing, transparent procurement and investment in energy infrastructure have helped create the foundations for further growth. Agrivoltaics can bring more of that opportunity into the rural economy, including work in installation, maintenance and agricultural services. Optimal crop selection is one of the prerequisites for the successful adoption of agrivoltaics. It should emphasise shade tolerance, morphological plasticity, and stable productivity under intermittent radiation. Appropriate agronomic management, including alley-based planting, adequate irrigation and nutrient supply, is essential for maintaining productivity. Agriculture and energy departments must plan together, with state governments, research institutions and local bodies. The farmer experiences the results of all these decisions on one holding. Our institutions should be capable of working with the same sense of unity. Farmer trust must guide every step. Cultivators should be able to understand an agreement, know the return they can expect and see who bears each responsibility. Land ownership must remain protected. Tenant cultivators and women farmers also need a voice in how projects are designed and how benefits are shared. India’s journey towards Viksit Bharat must be built on the prosperity of its villages. Under Prime Minister Leadership, empowering the annadata has been a central purpose of governance. India has valuable experience on which to build. ICAR’s Central Arid Zone Research Institute in Jodhpur has explored cultivation alongside solar generation and rainwater harvesting. BAIF’s Rural Innovation Centre in Pune is testing different configurations across a range of crops. The Government of India has established the Centre of Excellence (CoE) on Agri-Photovoltaics with 100 kW capacities at ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi in 2025. This is jointly led by ICAR and National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE) under the guidance of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy. The data generated from the CoE for the next two years will help in providing technical suggestions on specific crop suitability, boundary conditions and optimal integration of agricultural fields and solar panels. Hosting the world conference brings an international scientific community into this national endeavour. Affordable structures and finance suited to modest holdings deserve as much attention as advances in solar technology. This is also an opportunity to deepen India’s partnership with the Global South.

title: Test #25: Policy Coordination: Key to Good Governance
text: Public policymaking and implementation require multi-level planning and decision-making. This exercise becomes more complex and challenging in a country as vast and diverse as India. The Government of India, recognising the transformative power of sports in nation-building and holistic development, launched the Khelo Bharat Niti in 2025 with the aim of transforming India’s sports landscape. The government may plan a policy, but its success depends on many stakeholders—in this case, states, districts, local bodies, schools, coaches, families, and athletes. They all have different yet important roles to play. Families need to support a sports career for their children, especially their daughters; national or state governments need to encourage students, including specially abled students to take up sports; local authorities have the responsibility to maintain sports grounds or parks; scientists and innovators are expected to conduct research on better nutrition or equipment; and the Central Government has to visualise the importance of sports for holistic health as well as for international diplomacy. Thus, the success of a policy, like Khelo Bharat Niti 2025, depends on the coordination between various stakeholders. The policy document of Khelo Bharat Niti says, “Strengthening the sporting culture and ecosystem from the block level to the national level is a key focus of the Khelo Bharat Niti 2025”. At the national level, the role of the Union Government is primarily focused on providing the larger policy framework, including the policy objectives. Also, it is supposed to provide funding as well as identifying the sources of funding for its agencies located at lower vertical levels of states, districts and blocks. Khelo Bharat Niti mandates state governments to strengthen sporting ecosystems through initiatives such as ‘Model Sports State’. State governments are expected to host major national games and tournaments and attract private investments through the public-private partnership (PPP) model to build sports infrastructure. Similarly, individual districts are encouraged to become ‘Model Sports Districts’ by enhancing their sports capabilities. Further at the level of blocks, sporting programmes are to be organised on a regular basis to attract mass participation and facilitate talent scouting. Apart from the role of the government and its agencies, the Khelo Bharat Niti 2025 seeks an active role of private organisations and individual citizens as well. Private organisations can come forward to sponsor sportspersons and sports teams. They can invest in supporting scientific research programmes to develop better nutrition and equipment, and better medical facilities for sportspersons. Governance may sound like government, but it is more about how decisions are made, implemented, and connected to people’s everyday lives. Public policy provides an important link between governance and public life. Through public policies, governments decide how resources should be used and how public services should be provided. Elected representatives, government officials, local institutions, civil society organisations, researchers, the media, the private sector, and people, all have different but connected roles in good governance. People, therefore, have an important contribution to make in the process of governance. By voting, following laws, raising concerns, participating in public affairs, and giving feedback on government services, they can help improve the way public institutions function. In a democratic country like India, governance is guided by the constitution, which lays down the framework for governing the nation. Good governance is essential to strengthening democracy, promoting sustainable development, and ensuring national progress. It depends on transparent institutions, accountable leadership, active citizen participation, and a strong commitment to the rule of law. Public policy is integral to good governance. Good governance and public policy are crucial foundations for achieving national development goals.

title: Test #26: The Evolution of Camouflage & History of Art
text: As much as 48,000 years-ago, a cave painting in Indonesia shows, hunters wore animal skins and masks as camouflage. Thousands of years later, the trick would be used in war. Julius Caesar, invading Britain in the 1st-century BCE, reportedly used Venetian blue to coat ships, so they could scout without being too noticeable. Across millennia, the materials and methods have changed. These are now evolving beyond physical patterns, to embrace advanced materials and smart textiles so that they can account for drones, military VR headsets and smart surveillance systems too. In the 1890s, amid the Spanish-American War, painter Abbott Thayer tried to persuade the US government to use graded colours and tones for concealment, inspired by his study of how certain animals did this in the wild. The government remained unconvinced, but his work would lead other artists to create the early prints used during World War-1. As a result, he is considered the father of camouflage. It was the French army that first established a dedicated, secret unit clad in such gear, in 1915. (The word itself comes from the French “camoufler”, for “disguise”). In 1996, Canada launched the Canadian Disruptive Pattern or CADPAT, the world’s first digital variant. Unlike traditional camouflage, which use macropatterns with sharp outlines, this used macropatterns and pixelated micropatterns that blur together at a distance, causing visual dissonance and confusion. Roping in artists, set designers and sculptors, they created hooded smocks and painted rifles in drab green and brown, as well as fake trees that concealed sentry posts. By 1917, British lieutenant Norman Wilkinson had pioneered the idea of painting warships in bold, zigzag black-and-white lines, to distort perception of their size, speed and direction. This way, he reasoned, the enemy might find it harder to secure a direct hit. Dazzle camouflage became a pop-culture sensation too, turning up on dresses, shirts and swimwear. By World War-2, aircraft were being painted in darker earthy tones above and light tones below, to camouflage them against the ground and sky. By now, the armies of the US, UK, Germany, Italy and Russia had each created a range of prints for their uniforms, designed to suit various landscapes: snow, desert, forest, tropical jungle. The most widely used of these are the tiger stripes, French lizard, and the frog skin, that last one perhaps the most recognisable of all. The early Aughts marked the spread of such digital designs. Chief among these was the universal camouflage pattern (UCP), a pixelated bluish-grey print adopted by the US Army, but abandoned after it only served to highlight soldiers, against the dark mud and arid deserts of Afghanistan. By 2010, US troops had switched to MultiCam, which uses high-resolution, organic, flowing shapes to match textures of dirt, rocks and leaves, in shades of green, brown and tan. This is the most widely used type today, worn by police officers, SWAT teams and ICE agents too. Modern combat uniforms are often also treated with thermal coatings and passive emission barriers that absorb or mask body heat, blinding heat-sensing surveillance. A range of such artefacts are now on display at the International Spy Museum in Washington DC, where an exhibition titled Camouflage: Designed to Deceive opened in March and runs all year. By the 1960s, these patterns were entering the mainstream with an unlikely message: peace. Amid the Vietnam War (1955-75), veterans and protestors turned camouflage jackets into political statements, scrawling anti-war messages on them, adding anti-war badges and flowers. They would migrate from there into fashion, reimagined by Jean Paul Gaultier; worn by Madonna at the 2017 Met Gala (in an outfit designed by Jeremy Scott). “These designs are so ideologically charged that, even when worn as fashion statements, they could be read as an anti-war gesture aligned with anti-imperialist left-wing politics,” says Louisa Rogers, an assistant professor of fashion communications at Northumbria University, UK.

title: Test #27: Entrepreneurship – From Ideas to Startups
text: Entrepreneurs are curious individuals who see opportunities where others see challenges and turn that spark into action. Whether it is leading a business that manufactures drones for traffic surveillance or creating eco-friendly jute-bags that can replace plastic, an entrepreneur works hard, and is driven by passion and a commitment to creating value for society. Born in Punjab in 1898, Mohan Singh Oberoi faced hardships early in life when his father passed away while he was still an infant. Despite the risks, he believed in his vision. Through hard-work and determination, he transformed struggling hotels into successful businesses, and went on to build one of India’s largest hotel chains. His journey shows how entrepreneurship is not only about having a good idea. It involves planning, teamwork, decision making, and the effective management of different areas of the business. In 1934, he acquired his first hotel, and in 1943, he gained control of Associated Hotels of India. His business expanded further when the Oberoi Inter Continental opened in New Delhi in 1965. In 2001, the Government of India accorded him the Padma Bhushan. He passed away in 2002; by then, the Oberoi Group, named after him, had become one of the world’s most respected hotel brands. This is entrepreneurship, a process through which individuals, or a group of individuals, convert a potential idea into a business venture. Every great business starts with an idea, a need, or a desire to innovate and meet the needs of society. After somehow completing his education, he moved to Shimla and took a job as a hotel desk-clerk, earning just INR50 a month. Rather than limiting himself to his assigned duties, Mohan learned every aspect of hotel operations, from guest service to billing and administration. His dedication, curiosity, and willingness to take initiative set him apart. In 1934, he took a bold step by mortgaging his wife’s jewellery and investing all his savings to buy a small hotel. He established luxury hotels, founded a hotel management school, and expanded his business across the world. He hired and trained skilled staff to provide excellent hospitality services, and constantly worked to improve hotel facilities and guest experiences. He carefully managed the business’s finances to support growth and expansion. His hotels were renovated and operated efficiently to maintain high standards. The company built a trusted brand known for luxury and quality service. Customer satisfaction remained the top priority in all hotel operations. These are some of the functions that entrepreneurs and their teams perform. There are departments or groups within a company that focus on such distinct tasks and shared skills, also known as functional areas. Let us understand them in detail and learn how a business plan is prepared. A business plan provides a clear direction for turning an idea into a working enterprise. It describes the product or service, identifies potential customers, explains how resources will be arranged, and sets out the main activities needed to operate the business. Before starting a venture, entrepreneurs study customer needs, examine existing alternatives, and consider the challenges they may face. They also identify sources of finance and prepare a budget for equipment, materials, wages, transport, and other expenses. Proper accounting helps them record income and expenditure, monitor cash available for daily operations, and determine whether the business earns a profit or suffers a loss. Management and operations ensure that goods are produced or services are delivered efficiently, safely, and consistently. Human resource management involves selecting suitable employees, providing training, assigning responsibilities, and maintaining a supportive workplace. Marketing and sales help businesses understand customers, communicate the value of their products, and build lasting relationships. These functions must work together because even an innovative idea can fail without careful coordination.

title: Test #28: Coronary Thrombosis and Blood Clot
text: Coronary Thrombosis occurs when a blood clot forms in one of the arteries that supply blood to the heart muscle. These arteries carry Oxygen and nutrients that the heart needs to function. When a clot partly or completely blocks an artery, less blood reaches the heart muscle. This form of thrombosis is often associated with atherosclerosis, in which fatty deposits, cholesterol and other substances build up in the artery walls. These deposits, called plaques, can remain unnoticed for years. Breathlessness, sweating, nausea, dizziness and unusual fatigue may also occur. An Electrocardiogram (ECG) records the heart’s electrical activity, while blood tests measuring cardiac troponin can help identify damage to the heart muscle. The symptoms depend on the artery affected and the extent of the blockage. Some people may have less typical symptoms or no obvious warning signs before the blockage becomes serious. A clot that significantly restricts blood flow through a coronary artery may cause chest discomfort, pressure or tightness. Pain may spread to the arms, shoulders, back, neck or jaw. Symptoms alone cannot confirm coronary thrombosis; medical assessment and investigations are needed. Suspected coronary artery blockage accompanied by chest pain or breathlessness requires emergency medical attention. People living with coronary artery disease are at greater risk of coronary thrombosis because fatty deposits can build up in their arteries and trigger clot formation if a deposit ruptures. Smoking, high blood pressure, high LDL cholesterol, diabetes, physical inactivity and an unhealthy diet can increase the risk of developing this artery disease. Coronary angiography uses a contrast dye and X-rays to show the coronary arteries and identify the location and extent of a blockage. This can help doctors decide how best to restore blood flow. Other tests may be used depending on the patient’s condition. Treatment aims to restore blood flow and prevent the clot from growing or new clots from forming. The approach depends on the location and severity of the blockage and the patient’s condition. Angioplasty may be used to reopen the affected artery. A thin tube is guided to the blockage, where a small balloon is inflated to widen the artery. A stent, a small mesh tube, is often placed to help keep it open. Doctors may also use antiplatelet medicines, which reduce the tendency of platelets to clump together, and anticoagulants, which interfere with the blood-clotting process. In selected cases, clot-dissolving medicines may be used. Coronary artery bypass surgery may be considered when the pattern of blockage makes it a more suitable option. Preventing further clots involves managing the underlying risk factors and following the prescribed treatment plan. This may include controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, stopping tobacco use, maintaining physical activity appropriate to the person’s condition and taking prescribed medicines. If the blood supply is cut off for too long, the heart muscle can become damaged, leading to a heart attack. The severity depends on how much of the artery is blocked and how quickly blood flow is restored. When a plaque ruptures or its surface is eroded, platelets gather at the site and a clot may form. The clot can then obstruct blood flow, sometimes suddenly. Damage to the inner surface of an artery can trigger the process of clot formation. Additionally, at rupture, the material beneath the plaque’s surface comes into contact with blood, prompting platelets to gather and the clotting process to begin. A clot may grow quickly and block the artery. In some cases, a clot may form in an artery affected by other conditions, including inflammation or injury to the blood vessel. Older age and a family history of heart disease at a younger age are also risk factors. However it can occur even in people who have not been diagnosed with coronary artery disease. The underlying plaque build-up may have gone undetected until it triggers the formation of a clot.

title: Test #29: Legal - BHC First Appeal No. 892 of 2019
text: The respondent owned a commercial goods vehicle, a multi-axle freight truck bearing registration No. MH-09-CV-4120, insured comprehensively with the appellant insurer for an Insured Declared Value (IDV) of Rs. 18,50,000/-. On the night of 12th October, 2015, while parked securely at a transport logistics yard in Ichalkaranji, the vehicle was stolen by unidentified culprits. The respondent’s driver discovered the theft the following morning and immediately lodged an oral report at the local police station, culminating in the registration of First Information Report No. 184 of 2015 on 13th October, 2015 under Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 within twenty-four hours. After an exhaustive investigation, the police submitted a final untraced report under Section 173(2) Cr.P.C., accepted by the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class on 18th March, 2016. However, when the insured submitted the claim on 27th October, 2015, fourteen days after the incident, the insurance company repudiated the entire claim, asserting a fundamental breach of Condition No. 1 of the policy, which mandated immediate notice in writing to the insurer upon occurrence of any accidental loss or theft. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant insurance company contended that prompt intimation is a vital condition precedent. It was argued that delay deprives the insurer of its statutory opportunity to appoint private investigators and assist law enforcement in tracing the stolen vehicle. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent insured submitted that when an FIR is promptly registered, delay in reporting to the insurer cannot vitiate a genuine insurance claim. Dismissing the appeal, this Court holds that insurance companies cannot repudiate legitimate claims on hyper-technical procedural pretexts. In the authoritative Three-Judge Bench decision in Gurshinder Singh v. Shriram General Insurance Company Limited, reported in (2020) 11 SCC 612, affirmed in Jaina Construction Company v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd., reported in (2022) 4 SCC 527, the Hon’ble Supreme Court authoritatively settled the law. The Supreme Court established that the primary purpose of Condition No. 1 is to ensure that the theft is reported to the police without delay so that law enforcement can investigate the crime. When the insured immediately lodges an FIR, the police machinery is set in motion. The insurer’s investigator cannot do anything more than what the police do. Mere delay in communicating the theft to the insurance company after an immediate police FIR cannot be made a ground to repudiate a genuine total loss claim. In Om Prakash v. Reliance General Insurance, reported in (2017) 9 SCC 724, it was affirmed that a consumer cannot be deprived of statutory indemnity where the delay is explained by trauma and search efforts. The decree passed by the trial court directing payment of the full IDV with nine percent interest per annum is accordingly affirmed. Modifying the award, this Court holds that fixing a pittance as notional income of a homemaker offends constitutional equality and gender justice under Article 14 and Article 21. In the seminal ruling in Kirti v. Oriental Insurance Company Limited, reported in (2021) 2 SCC 166, the Hon’ble Supreme Court established that fixing the notional income of a homemaker is a recognition of the unpaid labor, time, and emotional sacrifices rendered to the family unit. The Court held that it is not necessary to produce documentary proof of income, and the notional income must be assessed on the basis of minimum wages applicable to skilled workers, taking into account the educational background and responsibilities of the homemaker. Furthermore, as reaffirmed in Arun Kumar Agrawal v. National Insurance Co. Ltd., reported in (2010) 9 SCC 218, and National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi, reported in (2017) 16 SCC 680, an addition of forty percent must be granted towards future prospects where the deceased was below forty years of age.

title: Test #30: The Trouble with Emotions
text: Our relationship with emotions is complex on one hand, they allow us to experience life, and on the other, they so often muddy our thinking and make us take decisions we regret. While we think often about our emotions, the more interesting question is why we have them at all? It is a strange faculty, if you think about it: this subjective infusion of feeling into behaviour. But we also know that emotions are awkward beasts. They arrive uninvited and complicate things. We understand physical reactions quite easily touching something hot sends pain signals to the brain. We understand the laws of physics: there is cause and effect at play here. But emotions confound us. For one, they are remarkably complex, often inarticulate and vary from person to person. The same piece of music can induce a sense of cosmic transcendence in one and stupefied boredom in another. The same movie can make someone cry, while the other person yawns and scrolls through scented candle options. At one level, we respond to the world through our emotions. Emotions create a relationship with the outside. Our feelings locate us with respect to events. Something happens, and we feel happy, frightened, angry or sad. We make sense of the world through our feelings. Events acquire significance and shape; they trig-ger reactions. Emotions tell us what we value, how much we value it, and what we are prepared to do to protect what we value. Mere information shorn of emotion, like directions to a destination, is useful, but major life decisions are determined by how we feel about things. We are afraid when we have some-thing to lose. We grieve when we lose someone whom we have included in the definition of the self. When we love, we give someone else a stake in us. We get angry when we are made to feel small. The world becomes a place full of meaning because of how we feel about what it throws at us. This is what makes emotion so individual. The instruments might be similar, the emotions themselves might be universal, but the manner in which we use them is dramatically different. What solitude means to me, how averse I am to small talk, how irritated I can be at the drone of a pompous speaker: these are all highly individual traits. Emotions are a bank, where we keep depositing experiences. We do not encounter the world afresh each morning. We carry within ourselves a compact-ed version of our experiences and how they made us feel. Failure in the past makes us wary of future initiatives. Be-ing let down or betrayed in something important makes trusting others difficult. The affection of strangers makes us more open to others. The past then shapes the future. We don't start afresh when we encounter a new situation. We like someone we meet for the first time, without quite knowing why. We get 'bad vibes' from an unfamiliar context. We embrace some situations and shun others, calling it instinct. Emotion here is a form of predigested knowledge, one that is not always correct. Over time, these set responses be-come what we think of as personality. We use them as labels to describe our-selves shy, gregarious, adventurous, wary, easily offended. When we say we know ourselves, we usually mean that we have a sense of how we react emotionally to events. Perhaps what we experience as a stable self is, in large part, e this pattern of response. Having a predictable way of reacting gives us a sense that there is someone fixed on the inside. And sometimes, we hold on to these patterns even when they are counter-productive. How we use language gives us a clue. We harbour a grudge, nurse a grievance as if it were a drink, breed discontent, foster a resentment, we rear enmity, the way one brings up a child. These are all words that connote caretaking, nurturing. Nobody says that we are harbouring contentment or nursing joy. Happiness carries us away; unhappiness is what we store. Sometimes, what causes us pain is precisely what we are most reluctant to surrender. This is why we fail so often when we try to console people.

title: Test #31: Kufri Jamunia - Biofortified Purple Potato
text: Biofortification improves the nutrient content of crops through plant breeding, enabling food to naturally provide higher levels of essential nutrients. Unlike conventional food-fortification, which adds nutrients during processing, biofortification integrates nutrition directly into the crop. Kufri jamunia represents an important advancement in the development of biofortified potato varieties in India. Kufri jamunia is a medium-maturing potato variety with medium-tall plants and a semi-compact canopy. The tubers are dark purple on the skin and purple in the flesh. They are oblong, with shallow eyes and a mealy texture. Each plant produces 10-12 medium to large tubers. Kufri jamunia contains 42.05 mg/100 g of anthocyanins in flesh and 80.66 mg/100 g in skin. It also contains around 42.75 mg/100 g of Vitamin-C in the flesh. This makes it a sustainable and cost-effective approach to improving nutritional quality in commonly consumed foods. It also strengthens long-term nutritional security. One important outcome of biofortification research has been the development of coloured-potato varieties with enhanced nutritional value. These include red, purple, and blue-fleshed potatoes. These potatoes contain natural pigments, such as Anthocyanins and Carotenoids, which give them their distinctive colours. Coloured-potatoes are rich in antioxidants and micronutrients such as iron and zinc. Hidden hunger remains a major public health challenge despite adequate calorie intake. It occurs when people consume sufficient food but lack essential vitamins and minerals in their diet. To address this challenge, scientists are increasingly developing biofortified crops with enhanced nutritional value. By combining good agronomic performance with enhanced nutritional quality, the variety offers benefits for both farmers and consumers. Its rich content of antioxidants, vitamins, and micronutrients makes it a valuable addition to efforts to improve dietary diversity and address hidden hunger. With its attractive appearance, culinary versatility, and adaptability to several states in the North Indian plains, Kufri jamunia has strong potential for wider cultivation and consumption in the future. Apart from its nutritional advantages, Kufri jamunia is suitable for a wide range of culinary applications. The variety is valued for its attractive purple colour, mealy texture, and pleasant flavour. This makes it suitable for both traditional preparations and processed food products. Its distinctive pigmentation also enhances the visual appeal of dishes and processed foods. In addition, the tubers can be processed into dehydrated products such as anthocyanin-rich daliya, suji, and flour, which can be used as ingredients in various food formulations. Potatoes are stuffed with phytonutrients, which are organic components of plants that are thought to promote health, according to the USDA. Phytonutrients in potatoes include carotenoids, flavonoids and caffeic acid. The vitamin C in potatoes acts as an antioxidant. These substances may prevent or delay some types of cell damage, according to the National Institutes of Health. They may also help with digestion, heart health, blood pressure and even cancer prevention. Purple potatoes are especially good sources of phytonutrients and antioxidants. A 2012 study published in the Journal of Agriculture and Food Chemistry found that six to eight small purple potatoes twice a day helped lower blood pressure and risk of heart disease and stroke among people who were overweight and suffering from hypertension. Despite the carbohydrates in purple potatoes, the participants did not gain weight. Potatoes may help lower blood pressure for several reasons. Jarzabkowski said that the fiber found in potatoes could help lower cholesterol by binding with cholesterol in the blood. Potatoes are also a good source of potassium. Brain functioning and nervous system The B6 vitamins in potatoes are critical to maintaining neurological health.

title: Test #32: The International Kullu Dusshera After Vijayadashmi
text: The International Kullu Dussehra, to be held from October 21 to 27, is a unique blend of religious faith, centuries-old traditions, cultural heritage, and tourism. Unlike Dussehra celebrations in most of the country, the weeklong festival in Himachal Pradesh’s Kullu valley begins on Vijayadashami, when celebrations elsewhere generally conclude. The festival’s origins date to the 16th-century-CE during the reign of Raja Jagat Singh, who ruled Kullu from 1637-1662. According to local tradition, the king brought an idol of Lord Raghunath from Ayodhya to get rid of a Brahmin’s sin and installed it at Sultanpur near Kullu on the occasion of Vijayadashami. He subsequently accepted the deity as the kingdom’s presiding lord, placing the royal authority under it. The annual congregation of local deities became central to the festival, with Dhalpur ground serving as the venue for their assembly over the course of a week. Lord Raghunath remains the principal deity, and other deities gather to pay obeisance to him. The ceremonial procession is accompanied by traditional drums, trumpets, devotees, and decorated chariots. Deities arrive from different parts of the Kullu valley, including Manali, Banjar, Anni, Nirmand, Sainj, Gadsa, and Manikaran. According to local tradition, the deities also visit Rupi Palace also known as the Sultanpur Palace to meet the erstwhile royal family. To promote local products, over a hundred stalls were set up by self-help groups in Kullu. Traders and artisans from neighbouring states, including Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan, are also coming. Devtas, considered to be living deities, are placed in huge traditional, decorated palanquins and chariots and then brought to Kullu’s Dhalpur ground. This year, the festival organiser International Kullu Dussehra Committee (IKDC) has invited a record 347 deities 63 more than the originally recognised 284 devi–devtas in the revenue record called Wajib-Ul-Arz, reflecting the expanding participation in the annual congregation. The arrival of deities at Dhalpur ground is expected to begin on Tuesday (October-20), with more reaching the venue by the morning of Wednesday (October-21). Their arrival marks the beginning of religious rituals and traditional festivities. Here’s what to know about the history and traditions of Kullu’s Dussehra celebrations, the increase in the number of deities, and the intertwining of the festival with politics. In 2021, UNESCO included Durga Puja in its Intangible Cultural Heritage list, recognising its growth as a global cultural platform. By the mid-1990s, economic liberalisation transformed urban spaces across Kolkata. A baseline study commissioned by the British Council estimated the creative economy surrounding Durga Puja in West Bengal at Rs 32,377 crore in 2019, a figure that has grown to an estimated 65,000 crore in later, broader trade assessments. This economic footprint is distributed across retail and fashion (accounting for nearly 35-40% of festive spending), food and beverage services, event production, creative design, and corporate media advertising. Corporate involvement in the festival initially relied on traditional banner advertising, gate sponsorships, and brand-sponsored award competitions. Recent years, however, have seen major changes. A clear example is the Adani Group’s Aagomoni initiative, which introduced direct structural grants of Rs 25-lakh each to eight selected puja committees across Kolkata, Bidhannagar and South Dum Dum. Out of these grants, specific funds were earmarked directly for artists, sculptors and lighting architects thus infusing corporate capital directly into the creative production process. Additionally, the introduction of curated, invitation-only “preview shows” prior to official public inaugurations points towards the emergence of an access economy tailored for crowd-free viewings. While the headlines focus on multi-crore budgets and corporate grants, the festival also functions as a vital micro-economic livelihood engine across multiple tiers of informal labour.

title: Test #33: History of the Jantar Mantar, Delhi
text: The Jantar Mantar in Delhi was built by Sawai Jai Singh-II, the king of Amer and one of the Mughal empire’s most important allies, on the orders of Emperor Muhammad Shah (1702-1748 CE), popularly known as “Rangeela” for his indulgence in arts, wine and music. It was the first of the observatories Jai Singh built. Most key observations were made here, forming the foundation for his new set of astronomical tables, the Zij-i Muhammad Shahi, named after the emperor himself. Historians do not agree on exactly when the observatory was built. According to Pandit Gokal Chand, its construction can be dated to 1710. Sayyid Ahmad Khan gave a later date of 1724, stating that the observatory was built on Muhammad Shah’s command in the seventh year of his reign, which corresponds to the Islamic year 1137 AH, or 1724-25 CE. According to J.R. Kaye in his work, The Astronomical Observations of Jai Singh, Jai Singh’s own writings help resolve this disagreement. He sought “to accomplish the exalted command (of emperor Muhammad Shah) he had received, he (Jai Singh) bound the girdle of resolution about the loins of his soul and built here (at Delhi) several of the instruments of an observatory.” Kaye explains that Jai Singh was encouraged by the emperor when he proposed preparing new astronomical tables. Determined to carry out this royal commission, he then built several observatory instruments in Delhi. This, of course, suggests that work began only after Muhammad Shah came to the throne, which rules out the earlier date of 1710. Jai Singh also says that the tables took seven years to be completed. In 1719, the same year the emperor took the throne, Jai Singh was appointed the emperor’s lieutenant in Agra, showing how closely he was tied to the imperial court at this time. A further clue comes from Jagannath, Jai Singh’s leading astronomer, who recorded observations taken in Delhi in 1729. Considering all this evidence, the most likely date for the founding of the Delhi observatory is around 1724. The design of the observatory reflects Jai Singh’s search for greater accuracy. By his own account, he first built brass instruments like the astrolabe (an early instrument used to observe and calculate the position of celestial bodies), following the specific methods described in Islamic astronomical texts. Kaye notes, this was similar to what “had been erected at Samarqand agreeable to the Mussalman books such as Zat al-Halqa of brass, in diameter three gaz of the measure now in use”. These, however, did not satisfy him. He therefore designed instruments of his own invention, including the Jai Prakash, the Ram Yantra and the Samrat Yantra. He built them out of stone and lime so that they would be completely stable and far more reliable than the metal versions. During Jai Singh’s lifetime, the observatory most likely included the Samrat Yantra (a massive sundial providing relatively precise measurements of time), the Jai Prakash (an elaborate sundial), the Ram Yantra (to measure celestial alignment), a mural quadrant and a number of metal instruments. Of the structures that stand today, the Misra Yantra or mixed instrument, may have been a later addition. It was possibly built by his son, Madho Singh, who is said to have inherited a good deal of his father’s passion for science. The Delhi observatory is mentioned quite often in the writings of travellers through the 18th and early 19th centuries, and several of these accounts are worth noting. In 1734, Father Claude Boudier and another priest passed through Delhi on their way to Jaipur. While there, they used the observatory to take readings of latitude and longitude. Unfortunately, they left no description of the observatory or its instruments during this trip. Further, in 1795, Franklin wrote about the observatory in his account of the city of Delhi. According to him, it was built in the third year of Muhammad Shah’s reign by Raja Jai Singh, who was helped by many well-known astronomers from Persia, India and Europe.

title: Test #34: Legal - PHHC Civil Writ P. No. 24812 Of 2018
text: The petitioner enrolled in the Punjab Police in 1994, completing over twenty-two years of disciplined service with fourteen commendation certificates and clean annual confidential reports. On 12th July, 2016, while deployed on security duty at a sensitive border post, the petitioner suffered severe acute lumbar radiculopathy and spinal disc herniation, rendering him completely bedridden and incapacitated. The petitioner was admitted to Guru Gobind Singh Medical College Hospital, Faridkot, where he underwent intensive traction and spinal rehabilitation until 4th October, 2016. The petitioner's family dispatched medical certificates and leave applications by registered post, but the department treated him as absent without leave, initiating a summary departmental inquiry under Rule 16.24. The inquiry officer conducted ex-parte proceedings without verifying the government hospital records, concluding that the absence was established. On that basis, the Senior Superintendent of Police passed an order of dismissal, holding that unauthorized absence in a disciplined uniform police force constitutes the gravest act of misconduct proving incorrigibility under Rule 16.2(1). Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner contended that the extreme penalty of dismissal is shockingly disproportionate and violative of Article 14 and Article 21 of the Constitution. It was submitted that absence occasioned by sudden medical incapacitation without willful defiance does not constitute the gravest misconduct. Learned State counsel defended the dismissal, submitting that in a disciplined police force, unapproved absence compromises border security, demonstrating unfitness for public service. Allowing the writ petition, this Court holds that Rule 16.2(1) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 requires a high threshold of culpability before stripping a police officer of livelihood and pension. In the landmark authority in State of Punjab v. Ram Singh, Ex-Constable, reported in (1992) 4 SCC 54, the Hon'ble Supreme Court established that dismissal under Rule 16.2 is reserved solely for the 'gravest acts of misconduct' or continued persistent misconduct proving incorrigibility and complete unfitness for police service. The word 'misconduct' implies a conscious, intentional transgression of duty. In Krushnakant B. Parmar v. Union of India, reported in (2012) 3 SCC 178, it was authoritatively settled that unauthorized absence cannot be treated as misconduct if it was due to compelling circumstances beyond the employee's control, such as certified illness. The petitioner was medically incapacitated in a tertiary government hospital, and the department produced no evidence to suggest that his medical records were fabricated. Dismissing an officer on the verge of pensionary retirement for involuntary medical absence is punitive and arbitrary. The impugned dismissal order dated 14th March, 2017 is quashed, directing reinstatement of the petitioner with continuity of service and fifty percent back wages. This civil writ petition, preferred under Article 226 and Article 227 of the Constitution of India, calls in question the legality, validity, and proportionality of the departmental punishment order dated 14th March, 2017 passed by Respondent No. 3, the Senior Superintendent of Police, Ferozepur, dismissing the petitioner from service as a Head Constable under Rule 16.2(1) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 on the ground of unauthorized absence from duty for eighty-four days, as affirmed by the appellate and revisional orders. Quashing the FIR and consequential proceedings, this Court holds that the search of a private vehicle is governed strictly by Section 42 and not Section 43 of the NDPS Act. In the authoritative Three-Judge Bench decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Boota Singh v. State of Haryana, reported in (2021) 19 SCC 606, the law was conclusively settled. The Supreme Court held that the Explanation to Section 43 defines a public place to include any public conveyance such as public buses, trains, or taxis;

title: Test #35: The Doctrine of Pith and Substance
text: The Doctrine of Pith and Substance represents one of the most vital principles of constitutional interpretation employed in federal and quasi-federal jurisdictions to preserve the delicate equilibrium of legislative competence between central and regional governing bodies. Originating in the nineteenth-century jurisprudence of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council while interpreting the distribution of legislative powers under the British North America Act of 1867 most notably articulated in decisions such as Cushing v. Dupuy and Russell v. The Queen the doctrine addresses the inescapable reality that complex modern legislation cannot always be compartmentalized into neat, water-tight constitutional compartments. This doctrine gained widespread prominence and rigorous institutional development in the constitutional jurisprudence of India, where it was extensively applied to resolve federal disputes under the Government of India Act of 1935 and subsequently embedded into the post-independence constitutional framework under Article 246. In the landmark case of Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce, Khulna (1947), the Privy Council upheld the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, which capped loan interest rates a topic of provincial competence regarding money-lending even though it incidentally affected negotiable instruments such as promissory notes, a field reserved exclusively for the federal legislature, because the dominant pith and substance of the law was agrarian debt relief rather than commercial banking. This judicial approach was reaffirmed and cemented by the Supreme Court of India in State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), where the Bombay Prohibition Act was sustained as a valid exercise of state legislative power over intoxicating liquors, despite incidentally affecting the importation and exportation of goods across borders, which constituted a central union subject. The doctrine functions not as an instrument to permit subversion of constitutional boundaries, but as a pragmatic rule of constitutional accommodation that recognizes the organic interconnectedness of contemporary socioeconomic life and prevents the paralysis of governmental functioning. It operates in close dialogue with related constitutional doctrines, contrasting sharply with the Doctrine of Colourable Legislation which invalidates laws where a legislature covertly accomplishes that which it cannot do directly and providing a crucial threshold inquiry before questions of repugnancy or direct statutory inconsistency arise. In the contemporary regulatory state, the Doctrine of Pith and Substance remains profoundly relevant in resolving jurisdictional friction over emerging digital economies, data privacy, environmental protection, and unified taxation regimes, ensuring that federalism remains dynamic, functional, and anchored in substantive legal reality. In federal constitutional systems featuring distinct legislative lists or enumerated fields of authority, such as those found in Canada, Australia, and India, a statute enacted by one tier of government under its legitimate constitutional mandate may inevitably touch upon, overlap with, or incidentally encroach upon a subject matter allocated exclusively to another tier. Rather than mechanically invalidating an enactment the moment an incidental overlap occurs, the Doctrine of Pith and Substance commands constitutional courts to scrutinize the enactment holistically to ascertain its true nature, character, and foundational essence—its "pith," meaning the true center or core, and its "substance," signifying its essential material reality. Under this interpretive methodology, if the substantive core, primary objective, and dominant effect of the challenged statute fall squarely within the legislative competence of the body that enacted it, the statute is upheld as constitutionally valid, notwithstanding the fact that it incidentally or tangentially trenches upon an unauthorized legislative head of power reserved for another legislature.

title: Test #36: Indian Democracy - Views of Voters & Experts
text: In its 2023 survey of 24 countries, Pew found that the median share of respondents who considered representative democracy to be a “good system” was 77%, while the median share dissatisfied with the way it was functioning was 59%. In Pew’s 2025 survey, 74% of Indian respondents said they were satisfied with how democracy was working the second-highest share among the countries surveyed. Citizens vote in the expectation that their representatives will make good their promises. When their representatives do the needful for instance, by abrogating Article-370 supporters see the fulfilment of a commitment, while critics see an abuse of power. Thus what appears a quintessentially democratic act to one side appears wholly undemocratic to the other. The difference boils down to what each side expects democracy to do. To the expert, democracy is more than a means of selecting rulers or resolving disagreements; it is also a means of managing power. But this is not how “experts” consulted by organisations like V-Dem and Freedom House see it. Citing concerns about press freedom, the treatment of Opposition figures, and the independence of investigative agencies, they argue that an excessive concentration of power has transformed Indian democracy into an “electoral autocracy”. When the persistence of the majority or the obstructiveness of the minority exhausts patience, a trial of strength looms. It is this foreboding that one is never far from open conflict that makes democracy less pleasant in practice than in theory. These paradoxes help explain the marked discrepancy between the views of ordinary citizens and those of experts when it comes to democracy in India. The discrepancy between the views of ordinary citizens and those of experts offers a useful illustration of why people disagree so sharply about democracy in practice. This disagreement can be traced to four paradoxes in democracy. The first concerns mandates. Citizens must rely on some method to make collective decisions. Since democracy assumes that individuals are equal, this method usually takes the form of voting in elections. This entitles the winner of an election to say that they have a mandate to govern. But no selection procedure is beyond question. For instance, money may give a party an unfair advantage over its rivals. Consequently, when individuals and groups dislike a policy that is being enacted by an elected government, they can question whether it “truly” embodies the will of the people. Meanwhile, elected officials take the opposite view that the mandate they have been given is being “sabotaged” by those who have lost the election, or worse still, by unelected bodies beholden to private or sectional interests. The second paradox concerns authority. Because unrestricted authority can lead to the abuse of power, democratic governments are subject to checks and balances. The idea is to compel even a government elected by a sizeable majority to slow down and build broad consensus. But this arrangement generates a dilemma. A government that fails to deliver what most voters want runs the risk of losing their support. Seeking to satisfy them, it will press against the limits of its authority, leading to accusations of overreach. The end result is disenchantment either of the majority, if the government dithers, or the minority, if it acts decisively. A third paradox relates to institutions. In the modern era, governance is conducted through a range of independent institutions. These institutions, such as universities, central banks, and regulators, are granted autonomy to insulate them from political interference. However, because they are staffed by people with ideas and interests of their own, their impartiality cannot be taken for granted. They are, therefore, subject to political oversight by elected officials. Consider what happens when a university offers a class on a topic, such as the “occupation” of Kashmir, that most of the electorate considers wildly improper.

title: Test #37: Ram, Lakshaman and the Celesial Arsenal
text: The morning after Tataka’s defeat, Rama and Lakshmana stand before Sage Vishwamitra at his hermitage. The atmosphere is tense. Gurudev, we have slain Tataka, but her sons, Maricha and Subahu, will not let this rest. They will come with a massive Rakshasa force, wielding terrible magic, to seek revenge. We must be prepared to defend the yajna. Vishwamitra: You are wise to anticipate their wrath, Rama. But you shall not face them empty-handed. Today, I grant you the ultimate celestial armoury. First, I bestow upon you Bala and Atibala. These are not physical weapons, but advanced metabolic bio-codes that will optimise your cellular energy. You will never feel fatigue, exhaustion, or hunger. Lakshmana: Perfect. We can fight for days without resting. Vishwamitra: Exactly. Next, you must understand Samhara, the withdrawal lore. Every action has a reaction. If you release a weapon of massive energy, you must know how to recall and neutralise that energy safely without destroying the environment. Scores of glowing weapons materialise in the air around them. Vishwamitra: Behold! The Dharma, Kala, and Indra Chakras harness the unstoppable power of time and weather. The Vishnu Chakra is the ultimate electromagnetic discus. Finally, the mind-controlling Sammohana and the atomic-level creator weapons: the Brahmashira and Brahmastra. Over a hundred celestial systems are now at your command. Use them with a cool mind. At dusk, the yajna is underway. Suddenly, the sky turns an unnatural purple. Lakshmana: The atmospheric pressure is dropping rapidly! Maricha and Subahu descend from the clouds with a roaring army. Maricha, using immense muscular force, hurls massive boulders and uprooted trees. Subahu, weaving dark sorcery, opens a localised portal in the sky and rains putrid blood, flesh, and filth on the altar. Rama (dodging a boulder): They are blinded by grief, Lakshmana. We took their mother from them. I know the pain of separation. I will not take their lives if I do not have to. I must separate them and give them a warning! Rama steps forward, tracking Maricha’s trajectory. He fires the Manavastra, a glowing arrow that strikes the air directly in front of Maricha and creates a massive, concentrated shockwave. The explosion of kinetic energy catapults Maricha into the sky and throws him into the ocean, a hundred leagues away. Enraged by his brother’s defeat, Subahu amplifies his attack. Rama (sad but resolute): He leaves me no choice. Rama releases the Agneyastra, the weapon of the Fire God. Blazing white-hot, the arrow cuts through the dark rain and strikes Subahu squarely in the chest. The intense cosmic fire instantly consumes Subahu and purifies the entire ritual ground in a blinding flash of light. Lakshmana: The leader has fallen, but the army is still advancing! Rama: Let us clear the field! Rama shoots the Vayavyastra, the wind missile, into the centre of the army. Upon impact, it manipulates the local air pressure, creating a high-speed vortex. A localised hurricane sweeps across the hermitage, blowing the Rakshasa army away. The sky clears. Vishwamitra smiles at the princes. Did You Know? Metabolic Efficiency: Vishwamitra gave the princes the power to ignore hunger and fatigue. In real science, scientists study extreme survival in animals (like bears hibernating or birds migrating thousands of miles) to understand how to optimise cellular metabolism and energy storage! Kinetic Propulsion: This uses Newton’s Third Law of Motion (For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction). Today, rockets and jet engines burn fuel to create high-pressure gas, which is then expelled at high speed to propel the vehicle forward. Thermal Purification: Fire is a chemical reaction (combustion) but when it gets hot enough, it enters the plasma state. Hospitals today use extreme thermal energy (incineration) to safely destroy biological hazards. Aerodynamics: Wind in our atmosphere is simply air rushing from a high-pressure zone to a low-pressure zone!

title: Test #38: Starlink and the Digital Sovereignty Question
text: APJ Abdul Kalam once recalled that after the 1998 nuclear tests, American sanctions led a US partner to withdraw from the Light Combat Aircraft’s flight-control programme. The partner retained Indian equipment, software, and technical information held at its premises. Digital sovereignty is not freedom from the world. It is the ability to keep essential services running when foreign-laws, suppliers, or sanctions restrict access to technology. The Institutions exercising that power must also answer to citizens, with remedies when digital systems deny them services or violate their rights. Territorial sovereignty has never insulated countries from economic pressure. Digital systems spread practical control across several countries. An Indian service may use American software and Taiwanese chips, with maintenance performed remotely and access controlled through licences issued abroad. Indian law may govern the service without ensuring continued access to the licences, updates, and support it needs. On September 21, 2026, the Delhi High Court ordered SAP India to restore software support to Nayara Energy. The Indian arm of the German software group had cited European Union sanctions against the refiner. Nayara had encountered a similar problem with Microsoft. In July 2025, the American company suspended digital services following EU sanctions against the refiner, whose shareholders include Russia’s Rosneft. The prospect of Starlink’s entry into India raises a similar question about connectivity. Satellite broadband could connect remote communities and provide backup when terrestrial networks fail. Ukraine offers a warning: Officials there said unannounced restrictions on Starlink connectivity disrupted military drone missions during Russian attacks. Data localisation establishes where information sits, without necessarily settling who can operate the system, repair move it elsewhere. Domestic production can improve our options, although reproducing every component would consume resources India needs for other priorities. Dependence becomes a sovereignty problem when an outside actor can interrupt an essential service, and India cannot restore it before serious harm follows. Geopolitics is changing the terms of India’s technology choices. American export controls affect access to advanced chips. Chinese mineral restrictions can unsettle manufacturing. EU regulations shape access to an important market. These instruments have different purposes and consequences, but their effect can be similar. An Indian firm may discover that access is conditional on decisions made elsewhere. Friendly relations cannot guarantee that a foreign supplier will remain free to serve Indian customers. A technology partnership needs attention to licensing conditions and plans for what happens if access is cut. Elon Musk said the US government controlled operating limits for Starshield, the military service. India’s civilian needs differ, but local ground stations would not ensure control over the network. Before essential services depend on it, India needs workable alternatives. India has faced such tests before. Indian teams completed the system through sustained development and testing, drawing on expertise and institutions built over many years. UPI demonstrates an ability to build digital public infrastructure at scale. Our software firms serve global markets; Indian engineers help develop technologies used worldwide. Such connections bring knowledge, income and influence. Restricting legitimate data flows or making useful foreign technology needlessly expensive could weaken the very institutions and businesses from which greater Indian capability must grow. Participation in global technology markets does not by itself give Indian firms control over the technology they use. More Indian research must move from papers and prototypes into products we can maintain and improve here. Subsidies should support demonstrable capacity, including the skills to keep systems running after the foreign supplier has left.

title: Test #39: Startups and Their Contribution to the Nation
text: India’s vibrant startup ecosystem is built not only on innovation but also on perseverance, determination, and the willingness to take risks. The remarkable growth of entrepreneurship can be seen in official records. Under the Startup India initiative, 20,282 startups were recognised in 2021, followed by 26,596 in 2022 and 34,842 in 2023. The number remained significant at 34,294 in 2024 and increased to 49,429 in 2025. These figures reflect the growing interest in entrepreneurship and the increasing importance of startups in India’s economic development. However, all entrepreneurs should be aware that there is a chance of their business ending in failure. While some startups grow rapidly, others struggle or even close down. As with other things in life, there is nothing wrong with failure if an honest effort has been made. Every unsuccessful attempt offers valuable lessons that help entrepreneurs improve their ideas and build stronger businesses in the future. With consistent hard work and perseverance, India has emerged as the third-largest startup ecosystem in the world, supported by its young and talented population. The startup world is growing rapidly, driven by creativity, digital technology, and increasing access to financial resources. By 2025, India had around 120 unicorns, which are startups valued at more than one billion dollars. These enterprises operate in exciting fields such as e-commerce (online shopping), fin-tech (digital payments), health-tech (online healthcare), and agri-tech (farming technology). Cities like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai, and Delhi NCR have become major startup hubs, attracting entrepreneurs, investors, and skilled professionals. Startups contribute to the nation by creating employment opportunities, introducing innovative products, and improving existing services. They encourage competition and motivate traditional businesses to adopt modern technologies. Many entrepreneurs identify everyday problems and develop affordable solutions that benefit ordinary citizens. For example, agricultural startups help farmers access market information, improve productivity, and connect directly with buyers. Similarly, educational technology companies make learning resources available to students in remote areas, while healthcare startups improve access to medical advice through digital platforms. Such innovations demonstrate how entrepreneurship can address social challenges while generating economic opportunities. Successful entrepreneurship requires more than an innovative idea. Entrepreneurs must prepare a practical business plan, arrange financial resources, understand customer needs, and manage business operations efficiently. They must also maintain proper accounts, control expenses, and develop effective marketing strategies. A business becomes sustainable when its products or services meet genuine demands and generate sufficient income to support continued operations. Teamwork, responsible leadership, and the ability to adapt to changing circumstances are equally important for long-term success. In recognition of entrepreneurship’s importance, the government has introduced initiatives such as Startup India, Make in India, and Digital India. These programmes encourage innovation, support business development, and promote the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat, which focuses on making India self-reliant through local production and technological advancement. Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) also play a significant role by supporting local industries, providing employment, and strengthening economic activity beyond major cities. Together, startups and traditional enterprises contribute to a more inclusive and competitive economy.
