title: Test #99: Gaining Knowledge via Quantum Entaglement
text: What is thought? It is a hologram produced via photons emitted in the synaptic cleft, an extremely small, 20-nanometre region between neurons where one neuron talks with another by exchanging neurotransmitters. These NTs are chemicals that are exchanged between neurons and once exchanged; they are converted into electrical signals inside the neuron for the onward journey. A large number of such neuron interactions produce neural pathways, and each set of such neural pathways is responsible for the thought production of a particular object. During this exchange of neurotransmitters, weak photons, also called biophotons, are produced at each synaptic cleft. The synchronization of millions and millions of such synaptic cleft photons produces a hologram, which we can call thought. Most of these holograms are continuously produced in the brain. When the focus is not there, they also fade immediately. This is called brain chatter and is the genesis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, ADHD. However, a concentrated thought hologram, which, according to Sage Patanjali, results in Sanyam, concentration, focus, and Samadhi, has enough energy to be transmitted out of the brain; it is what we call a leaky thought. This thought hologram interacts with the object or subject of our interest and gets its knowledge. How does this interaction take place, and more importantly, how do our brains receive this knowledge? For objects that we can see and feel, it is quite easy because our senses guide through hologram in doing so. But for concepts and subjects that we do not see and are beyond our reach, what is the mechanism? The science of quantum entanglement may provide a possible answer. Quantum entanglement spooky action at a distance, as Einstein described it states that photons or even particles created or generated are entangled with each other in such a manner that knowledge of one can describe the other, no matter how far apart they are. We can conjecture that our concentrated thought hologram, which leaks out of the brain and interacts with the object or subject of our interest, somehow changes the property of hologram in the brain via the entanglement process. This continuous exchange of information through quantum entanglement allows ideas and reality to match in an induced-fit arrangement; thus, knowledge is perceived. The induced-fit model is used in drug design and is based on the hypothesis that the drug binds to the active site; in the process of binding, changes the shape of the active site to achieve a precise fit. This enhances drug action. The same action of induced fit may occur in hologram interaction with the object of interest, affecting the hologram in the brain. Sage Patanjali has also alluded to this mechanism in his Yoga Sutras. All great discoveries such as Einstein’s theory of gravitation; Newton’s theory of light, gravity, motion; music of Beethoven, Mozart among others, and knowledge of the universe by sages and scientists have been obtained by this process. However, when our senses do not feel and guide thoughts, yet knowledge is perceived, it can happen only through quantum entanglement of thought.

title: Test #100: SSC Typing Passage - The Families of Labourers
text:
You will find that a very few industrialists really look into the different welfare aspects of the labourers. Take the example of families and children of the labourers. Do their employers make proper arrangement for their health care and education; leave aside their cultural upliftment or their cultural life? The families of the labourers are not looked after properly and a great deal needs to be done and in this regard voluntary organisations can play some role. A small amount has been provided for the welfare of children and women in the unorganised sector. I would urge upon the hon. Minister that the allocations to the voluntary organisations for the betterment of women and children in the organised as well as unorganised sectors should be increased. Sir, as regards the lockouts, wherever there is a lockout of the industry, the labourers have a great deal of suffering. They do not know what to do. They are just left to their lot. But the employer does not suffer as such. Just look at the employers of different big industries. Their standard of living does not change after locking the industry but the people in the factories are left on the street. I suggest that whenever the question of lock-out in a particular industry comes up, the question should be considered whether the labourers will be able to run a particular industry and a lot of consideration should be given to this particular aspect and, if possible, that particular industry should be kept alive. Sir, migration is a very important problem of labourers and it has got multi-dimensions, that is, labourers within the country and those who are going outside the country. Lot of labourers is exported outside the country and they are facing lot of problems because of the agencies. I would like to mention here one thing that we have entrusted this work to many of the private agencies. But there is need to consider whether we can have a manpower corporation and assign this work to the corporation. Also, there are problems of inter-State migration of the labourers. There is an Act but it is causing difficulties to the labourers who migrate to other States. Assessing whether existing rates are sufficient to meet the needs of workers and their families can be challenging. First, needs of workers and their families cannot be considered in a vacuum; they must be understood in relation to a country level of economic and social development, taking into account the views of social partners.

title: Test #101: What's India's Best Foreign Policy
text:
Going purely by decibels on TV screens and social media, it would seem India in a constant state of geopolitical siege. Bangladesh has had a street enforced regime change replacing an India-friendly PM and Sri Lanka has thrown a surprise by electing a left-wing president. Border stand-off with China continues, even though there have been some conciliatory noises lately. Cherry on the cake has been the very public fracas with Canada. Rise of new powers has always been a messy affair, from the Peloponnesian war that marked the rise of Sparta at the expense of legacy power Athens to the Cold War which was cold only in the Western hemisphere. American scholar John Mearsheimer argues, the system is anarchic, great powers possess some offensive capabilities, no state can be certain of others intentions, survival is the primary goal, and actors are rational. Ergo, great powers fear each other and try to enhance their security by contesting aggressively to maximize their share of power and influence. Outside of arcane academic theories as well, the principles are well embedded in popular consciousness. In 2014 NYT published a cartoon illustrating India first Mars mission, showing a dhoti-clad man with a cow knocking at the door of a room marked Elite Space Club where two men in bowties sat reading a report on the mission. At one level, it was only a culturally offensive meme. But at a deeper level, it showed the hostility of the current establishment towards an emerging power. Rise of China, facilitated by the West since Nixon famous trip to Beijing in 1972, has been truly peaceful, till recently. But it has been an outlier exception, of a type never seen before, an outcome of a series of lucky coincidences in world politics. Every time an ostensibly unfriendly government comes to power in the neighborhood, the common refrain is India has lost the country. As if India could have, with greater diligence, either maintained Sheikh Hasina in power or crafted a peaceful transition to a friendlier alternative. In the last six years, Maldives has been lost and won about thrice. As Bill Clinton election campaign said, it the economy, stupid! title: Test #102: Full Scale Patrols In Demchok
text:
Army has kicked off full-scale patrolling at Demchok in eastern Ladakh, while it will soon follow suit in Depsang Plains after initial patrols in the area verified that People Liberation Army (PLA) had completely dismantled its temporary structures and pulled back its troops to pre-April 2020 positions. The patrolling is being conducted after informing PLA in advance as per the terms of the Oct 21 pact on patrolling arrangements, which led to disengagement in the remaining two of the seven major face-off sites that arose after multiple Chinese incursions into eastern Ladakh in April-May 2020. Our patrols now have full unrestricted access to the five patrolling points in Depsang and two in Demchok, which was earlier blocked by Chinese soldiers. PLA, too has begun its own patrols with prior information to us to prevent the possibility of any clash, a defence source told on Friday. As part of the initial patrols, Indian soldiers went up in Depsang Plains for the first time in almost five years through the Bottleneck, an area around 18km inside Indian territory which had been blocked by PLA. The patrols at Depsang and Demchok will be determined by our operational requirements and tasking, the source said. The longer duration patrols with more distance to cover will have 20-25 armed soldiers, while the shorter ones will have 10-15 soldiers. Depsang, a table-top plateau at 16,000 feet, is part of India vital Sub-Sector North, which includes the Daulat Beg Oldie airstrip, and strategically located near the critical Karakoram Pass in the northernmost part of eastern Ladakh. China claims almost all the 972 square km of territory in the Depsang Plains, where both sides have vast overlapping claims. Depsang, where tanks can operate, is far more impo rtant than other areas like Pangong Tso in eastern Ladakh. It is the only place where our PPs fall short of our perception of LAC. In other places, the PPs are almost bang on LAC, another source said. At the Charding Ninglung Nallah track junction near Demchok in the south, Indian troops will now access two important PPs, while villagers can also go to their traditional grazing grounds there. Troops will be able to patrol till Charding La, which is over 19,000 feet, the source said. After stabilisation at Depsang and Demchok, India focus will shift to the restoration of patrolling rights in areas where no patrol buffer zones were established after previous rounds of disengagements till Sept 2022. These buffer zones at Galwan, north bank of Pangong Tso, Kailash Range and the larger Gogra-Hot Springs area, largely came up on what India considers to be its territory.

title: Test #103: Parents Can Enroll For Ayushman Schemes
text:
Those aged 70 years and above can now benefit from the expansion of the Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) regardless of income, a major shift in the govt policy. Earlier, only poor and vulnerable families and a few specific categories of workers, like ASHA staff, were eligible for the scheme that offers health cover of Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary-care hospitalisation. Anyone aged 70 years or above can apply for the Ayushman Bharat Senior Citizen Scheme on the website, by using the Ayushman App (available for Android on the Google Play Store). Beneficiaries simply need to verify their identity and eligibility through Aadhaar e-KYC. Aadhaar serves as the primary document for confirming both the beneficiary age and state of residence and is the only document required to complete the registration process. Yes, Family members can register the eligible beneficiary through beneficiary login option on the mobile app and website. All they must do is to enter their mobile number and put in the OTP that generated to initiate the enrolment process. One can also visit the nearest empanelled hospital and get themselves enrolled. AB PM-JAY is a completely cashless scheme, and govt sources said payments are made to hospitals against the treatment provided to eligible beneficiaries. Empanelled hospitals are mandated to offer cashless treatment to beneficiaries. One can lodge grievances on the AB PM-JAY website or through the national call centre 14555, mail, letter, fax etc. Any complaint regarding denial of treatment by an empanelled hospital is to be seen as an SOS grievance and a turnaround time of 6 hours has been set for resolving it. Such beneficiaries will have to re-initiate their Aadhaar based e-KYC via the website or mobile app to be registered as a beneficiary under the senior citizen scheme. The list of empanelled hospitals for Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY scheme is available on the website. As of Sept 30, approximately 30,000 hospitals across the country are empanelled to provide benefits under the scheme, which is run overall by the National Health Authority. The list includes 190 leading corporate hospitals. Public health and hospitals being a state subject under the Indian Constitution, state health agencies (SHAs) are mandated to empanel hospitals under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY. Beneficiaries can visit any empanelled hospital, present either their Ayushman card or their PMJAY ID to receive treatment. Before visiting, the beneficiary should confirm that the hospital is empanelled to treat the specific condition for which they require assistance.

title: Test #104: 40 Years Later, Wounds Raw, Eyes Brimming
text:
Sobbing inconsolably, Nirmal Kaur and Pappi stand in a room filled with hundreds of photographs of men young, old and some of them, innocent children. The two women, now in their late 50s, were teenagers when their fathers and other family members were killed some burnt alive, others brutalised with knives and rods and left to die on the streets by mobs in Nov 1984 in what is considered one of the bloodiest communal massacres in Indian history. It will be 40 years since the riots against Sikhs across India following the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi by her Sikh bodyguards on Oct 31, 1984. The frenzy went on till Nov 3 when peace was finally restored. The murderous days were marked by mass killing, rapes, arson, acid attacks, immolation and extensive loss of property, with hundreds left homeless. For the elderly widows, middle-aged children and the grandchildren of those killed in the violence, this time of the year is a reminder of how their family lives changed forever. With Diwali in the air, just as it was 40 years ago, a space in west Delhi that is now associated with the turbulent journey of the survivors of the riots and home to the families that were rehabilitated after the riots. A dusty road leads one to the matchbox houses of C block that many in the locality refer to as Vidhwa Colony. The families resent this because of the stereotyping. But for decades they have told and retold their stories to police, politicians, enquiry commissions, rehabilitation committees and hordes of journalists. After all this, the reality continues to be grim. Just as the shrieks for justice and punishment to the guilty regularly erupt from homes there, their wretched lives are aggravated by the sheer civic neglect of their locality. The roads are eroded, the unkempt parks have turned into garbage dumps, houses are chipping with decay and families have outgrown the allotted refuge in the years since the riots. On a muddy lane with rundown tenements bearing nameplates of the men who died in the riots, one finds Chammni Kaur outside her dilapidated house. She is nearly 80. Her husband, Inder Singh, was a sewadar in the gurdwara in Block 32 of east Delhi Trilokpuri. Their happy family life ended on the morning of Nov 1 when the gurdwara was set afire. Kaur breaks down as she remembers how they huddled inside their house in fear while the mob killed her husband and her eldest son, Manohar Singh who was not even 18 yet.

title: Test #107: Memories Of a Terrible Day
text:
But on Oct 31, the matinee show at 3pm was half empty. The news was not yet out officially but everyone seemed to know of the attempt on PM Indira Gandhi life. An air of uncertainty prevailed. Everyone wondered whether she would survive. Even during the interval, one could hear gatekeepers discuss the news in hushed tones. By the time I came out of the theatre, All India Radio had announced the news of Indira assassination by her Sikh bodyguards. The road was choked. Vehicles honked madly, an uncommon occurrence those days. Everyone looked dazed and confused. The winter was slowly setting in and it was completely dark around 6.30pm. I walked to the nearest bus stand. About 60-70 passengers were waiting for DTC buses, the primary mode of public transport those days. There were none. After a 45-minute wait, 521, which took you to Super Bazar in Connaught Place, came. It was packed but some of us managed to squeeze in. A young woman in salwar-kameez was crying like a child. She kept on repeating, Ab desh kaise chalega? Who will run the country now? Others kept nodding in affirmation and baying for the blood of Khalistanis. The three or four Sikh passengers looked extremely worried. When the bus reached near Kotla, we had a first glimpse of what lay in store. The air was thick with black smoke. From Kotla to Janpath, dozens of cars and scooters were either in flames or lying abandoned. The brave driver kept changing the route to reach the destination. After every few minutes one could see belligerent crowds with sticks and bats on the road stopping vehicles. Little before the swank Le Meridien Hotel on Janpath, arsonists stopped our bus. They hurled abuses against Bhindrawale and Khalistanis. They did not cover their faces. They moved menacingly from one end of the bus to another in search of prey. Thankfully, the Sikh passengers had got off earlier. A car passing by told our driver to avoid going to CP, barely half a km away. No bus and no auto-rickshaws either I was stranded and scared. I walked to CP. Designed by British architect Robert Tor Russell, CP was named after Prince Arthur, the first Duke of Connaught and a grandson of Queen Victoria. Since its completion in 1933, it had been the capital finest shopping and business district and a premier attraction for tourists. That night it looked so different. Many shops were on fire. The streets were littered with stones and shattered glass. Vehicles burnt like paper. Stench of smoke filled the air. Law and order had surrendered to the merchants of death, who were calling the shots. Not a single cop was seen.

title: Test #108: Cosmic Wisdom and Holistic Wellness
text:
Deepavali, the Festival of Lights, is more than an occasion for festivities; it holds a profound blend of cultural, spiritual, and scientific meaning. Emphasising renewal, mental clarity, and unity, Deepavali rituals such as lighting diyas, oil lamps, fasting, and home cleansing promote well-being on multiple levels. Deepavalis tradition of light overcoming darkness reflects hope, resilience, and positivity. Psychologically, rituals like lighting diyas foster mindfulness, creating a space for grounding and reflection, much like mindfulness based therapies that help with focus and positive thought patterns. The practices of giving, sharing, and gratitude during Deepavali increase happiness, reduce stress, and strengthen bonds. Social connections during Deepavali boost oxytocin a hormone linked to trust and love helping to ease loneliness and increase life satisfaction. Fasting and home cleansing during Deepavali bring physical and mental benefits. Fasting supports metabolic health, reduces inflammation, and enhances cellular repair through autophagy, lowering risks for chronic diseases like diabetes and heart conditions. Similarly, cleaning the home reduces dust and allergens, benefiting respiratory health and contributing to mental well-being by linking cleanliness to happiness. In certain regions, Deepavali coincides with Kali puja, honouring Goddess Kali. This ritual brings powerful symbolism for transformation and resilience, encouraging us to confront fears and renew our inner strength. Goddess Kali fierce imagery embodies courage, helping us break free from negativity a theme reflected in therapy, where confronting fears leads to personal growth. The symbolism of Goddess Kali who embodies both destruction and creation parallels the cosmic phenomena of black holes and white holes, which represent the universe most extreme examples of these forces. By examining these cosmic entities, we gain insight into Kali role in guiding us through inner transformation, personal growth, and renewal. A black hole is a region in space with an immensely powerful gravitational force that pulls in everything around it, including light, rendering it invisible to the outside universe. In the context of Kali symbolism, the black hole represents her ability to absorb and neutralize negativity, fear, and ego. Just as a black hole consumes matter, Kali energy is believed to consume the obstacles that hinder self-growth and spiritual progress. She embodies the aspect of destruction that clears away the toxic elements within us, such as anger, greed, attachment, and other forms of darkness. This process, while intense and challenging, is transformative because it allows individuals to shed what no longer serves them, making room for something new. In this sense, Kali, like the black hole, symbolises a necessary phase of destruction that ultimately leads to transformation and renewal.

title: Test #110: Why Diwali Doesn't Mean Joy For Pets
text:
The sudden, intense sounds generated by fireworks can trigger profound distress and anxiety in dogs and other animals. Animals may experience elevated heart rates, uncontrollable shaking and fear. The loud noises can potentially damage hearing in animals too, and in some cases, make dogs go blind. Veterinarian Piyush Patel, director, Companion Animals and Engagement Team, Humane Society International India, said it was essential for pet parents to create a calm environment for their animals during noisy festivals like Diwali. On Diwali, many pets experience heightened stress and anxiety due to the loud noises from fireworks. This can lead to fear, disorientation, and even physical distress. The bright lights and chaotic celebrations can overwhelm pets, causing them to seek refuge or escape. Calming your pets during Diwali can make a big difference to their comfort. Dr Abhijit Pawde, head, Centre for Wildlife, Indian Institute of Veterinary Research, Bareilly, said, We have seen some cases in which dogs suffer from optic amaurosis disease, in which the animal loses eyesight due to the noise when crackers are burst close to their ears. Some people with malicious intent light the crackers near the ears of dogs. He added that the constant bursting of crackers creates panic among animals, who blindly try to run away and could end up being crushed by moving vehicles. Few animals become overaggressive and because they are uncomfortable with crackers, they try to attack and bite the fireworks. This can result in fractures or shattering of their jaw. Veterinarians said it was necessary to set up a quiet, cosy space for pets on such occasions, ensuring their bed, blankets and toys were near. They advise keeping pets away from windows and doors to help muffle noise and the use of rugs and carpets to absorb sound. Do not leave pets alone during the peak bursting of crackers and spend time with them, offer them cuddles, and if they show any signs of distress, consult a veterinarian, they prescribed. Delhi govt has imposed a complete ban on all fireworks this year. Ambika Shukla, trustee, People for Animals, has appealed to people to adhere to the pyrotechnics ban. If you have pets at home or you take care of community dogs, patrol your neighbourhood and report to the authorities if the ban is flouted, suggested Shukla. She added that dogs should be fed and taken for a walk before 5pm on Diwali before the cracker bursting begins and to ensure to put a name tag and contact number on the collar in case the animal flees in panic.

title: Test #111: More Migrants, Not Kids
text:
Last week, Andhra CM Chandrababu Naidu urged couples to have more children to fight the burden of an ageing population in the state. The next day, his counterpart Tamil Nadu CM Stalin invoked a Tamil saying a large family is a happy family to ask his people to adopt a large family norm. Although the two chief ministers nuanced the issue differently, the underlying message was unmistakably clear: Dont penalise states that have succeeded in population control. If you do, we have no alternative but to grow our populations. So, what exactly is the grievance of states successful in population control? It straddles both politics and economics. There are several routes through which central resources flow to states. The most structured of these is finance commission transfers whereby the Centre gives away 41% of its tax pool to states. Horizontal distribution of this pool across states is done by a formula in which most variables are scaled by population the larger a state population, the higher its share. Finance commissions, appointed once every five years, have historically been mandated to use the 1971 population numbers so as not to give a perverse incentive to states to neglect family planning with an eye on a higher share of tax devolution. This long-standing norm was changed when the 15th finance commission appointed in 2017 was asked to use the 2011 population numbers in its assessment of a state expenditure needs. States that had done well in stabilising populations, typically the southern states, protested this change in the base year calling it a penalty for good performance. Possibly taking a lesson from that, the 16th finance commission appointed last year hasn’t been given any specific mandate on what population figures to use. It is very unlikely though that they revert to the 1971 figures. The second major route for central resource support to states is Centrally Sponsored Scheme. Here again, the share of a state in the total CSS pool is largely driven by its population although in a less structured way than finance commission transfers. Central public investment via soft infra (example: an IIT or an AIIMS) and hard infra (example: roads, ports) is another major route for central resource flow to states. This is the most politically driven segment of central support and is obviously influenced by vote banks. States with larger populations tend to corner more benefits. title: Test #112: Legal Matter - Advt. Issued by UPPRPB
text:
Challenge in the present special appeal is to the judgment and order passed by the learned Single Judge of this Court in Writ appeal No. 17576 of 2019, whereby the writ petition has been dismissed. The matter pertains to the Male and Female Constable Recruitment 2018 initiated pursuant to an advertisement issued by the Uttar Pradesh Police Recruitment and Promotion Board. The principal relief sought in the writ petition was for a direction to the respondents to permit the petitioner to re-appear in the re-medical examination and further that a seat may be reserved for him until his grievance is redressed by the respondent authorities. Learned counsel for the appellant writ petitioner has tried to assail the judgment under appeal by contending that after being declared medically unfit by the Medical Board and also by the Appellate Medical Board, the petitioner had raised a claim for re-medical examination but the same had not been considered by the authorities. Learned Standing Counsel appearing for the State respondents has supported the judgment of the learned Single Judge by submitting that the petitioner having been declared medically unfit by a duly constituted Medical Board and the said finding having been affirmed by the Appellate Medical Board, there was no further provision for re-medical examination, and the writ petition had rightly been dismissed. We have heard the counsel for the parties and perused the record. The scope of interference in matters relating to assessment of fitness by a Medical Board constituted under the statutory rules in exercise of powers under writ jurisdiction, in our opinion, would be extremely limited. The Courts have, time and again, emphasised the need for caution when candidates seek to assail the correctness of the findings of a Medical Board constituted under a recruitment process adopted by the State authorities. We may observe that although the powers of the Court under Article 226 are wide enough to issue directions in appropriate cases but such powers are required to be wielded with caution and circumspection. Matters relating to the medical evaluation of candidates in a recruitment process involve expert determination and the Court should exercise caution in supplanting the process adopted by the recruiting agency and substituting it by a Court mandated further medical evaluation. Any such exercise in acceding to requests of candidates who are not found to be medically fit for reassessment on the basis of procedures other than those envisaged by the recruiting agency under the relevant rules would result in the recruitment process being derailed, which would ordinarily be not permissible. In a case where the recruitment process has been carried out as per prescribed statutory rules where under a procedure has been prescribed for testing the medical fitness of candidates by a duly constituted Medical Board, the report of the Medical Board is not to be normally interfered with, solely on the basis of a claim sought to be set up by a prospective candidate.

title: Test #114: Bhartiya Nyay Sanhita, 2023 - 2
text:
The IPC states that any act performed by a person of unsound mind does not constitute an offence.  The BNS retains this provision, except that it replaces the term unsound mind with mental illness. It states that mental illness is as defined in the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (MHA, 2017). The MHA, 2017 defines mental illness as a substantial disorder of thinking, orientation or memory that grossly impairs the capacity to recognise reality. The definition explicitly excludes mental retardation or incomplete development of mind from mental illness. Using this definition of mental illness to exempt someone from criminal responsibility may deny persons suffering from mental retardation protection from trial. The Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1972 was amended in 2008 to require a clinical test of whether the person was suffering from unsoundness of mind or mental retardation (both could be used as reasons to acquit the person). The definition of mental illness under MHA, 2017 also includes abuse of alcohol and drugs as a form of mental illness. Therefore, if an alcoholic commits an offence while intoxicated, he may be able to claim the defense of mental illness. This defense may apply even if he voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs. This contradicts the general defense of intoxication under the IPC, which only exempts acts committed under involuntary intoxication from criminal responsibility. The Standing Committee on Home Affairs (2023) recommended reverting to the term unsound mind. The BNS adds terrorism as an offence. It defines terrorism as an act that intends to: threaten the unity, integrity, and security of the country, intimidate the general public, or disturb public order. Terrorist acts include: using firearms, bombs, or hazardous substances to cause death, danger to life, or spread fear, or destroying property or disrupting essential services. By including the intention to disturb public order as a terrorist act, a wide range of offences may be classified as acts of terrorism. These may range from armed insurrection and war against the state to rioting and mob-violence. The Supreme Court (1960) has held public order as the absence of disorder caused by breaches of peace at the local level. It differentiated such disorder from national upheavals such as revolution, strife and war, which risk affecting the security of the state. Under the BNS, terrorist acts also include intimidating the general public. The Standing Committee on Home Affairs (2023) suggested defining intimidation to resolve ambiguities in categorizing terrorist acts.

title: Test #115: Learn AI To Secure Tech Career
text:
In this era where AI is transforming industries at unprecedented speed, the question isnot whether AI will transform work its how professionals can stay ahead of the curve. At our webinar last week, industry leaders shared insights on navigating the AI revolution and future-proofing talent. Change is nothing new to tech talent. He said the impact of AI is role-specific, with different implications for every role, be it product manager, developer, architect, or UX analyst. He advised techies to begin by harnessing AI in their personal lives, such as using language models for recommendations or data cleaning. This hands-on approach, he said, helps build an intuitive understanding of when and how to use AI in professional settings. Bikramjit Debnath, country head of Azure at Microsoft India, noted how AI is disrupting software development, with tools like GitHub Copilot generating millions of lines of code and boosting developer productivity. He said developers now need interdisciplinary skills, not just technical expertise. Developers need to combine AI plus domain knowledge, plus cloud knowledge, and also have a good understanding of cybersecurity, said Debnath. Raunaq Lalwani, VP of software said the company began experimenting with AI tools and techniques while simultaneously streamlining development processes. This approach, he said, led to the creation of SmartPal, an internal tool that uses AI to extract insights from unstructured data like case studies and capability presentations. The real-world impact of AI tools has proven significant. In one of Cybage greenfield projects, the team using GitHub Copilot achieved 26% higher average story points per hour compared to the team not using it. Lalwani said everyone must start using AI, understand it, find the right use cases, build a prototype, show it to stakeholders, get buy-in, and then build iteratively. AI, Debnath said, will make it easier for people to do everything better, faster, and cheaper. Microsoft ambition, he said, is to put an AI copilot in every pocket. He envisions AI companions for professionals across industries developers, lawyers, doctors, teachers, bankers, and even machine operators. We design AI to augment, not replace, human capabilities, he noted. This transformation will require significant investment in talent development though. Debnath pointed to Microsoft initiative to skill two million people in India by 2025. Nathani advocated for partnership between the tech industry, government, businesses, academia, and civil society to develop appropriate regulations that keep pace with AI rapid development. He cautioned against both over-regulation and under-regulation of AI use cases.

title: Test #116: Choose Forgiveness, No Matter The Challenge
text:
Unforgiveness is a sin and displeases God. He takes it seriously, even if we tolerate it in our hearts. When someone injures us, whether intentionally or inadvertently, we face a decision. This choice is entirely ours to make. We must decide whether to forgive or not. While much can be said about sin, one thing is certain it hinders us from experiencing God best in our lives, according to Mark. Do we ever ponder what our unforgiving hearts cause us to miss? By Divine grace, let us strive never to ask this question because we consistently opt for forgiveness, no matter the challenge. David deep faith in God forgiving nature defined him. A prominent figure in the Bible, David is known as a shepherd, poet, and giant slayer remember the David and Goliath story king and ancestor of Jesus. He lived passionately and sinned often but quickly confessed and repented sincerely. Despite his admirable qualities, he was also a betrayer, liar, adulterer, and murderer. One sin David regretted was his affair with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband to hide his wrongdoing. He acknowledged the pain caused too many. Yet, according to Psalm 51, God forgave him due to his genuine repentance. David valued God forgiveness and never took it lightly. No sin is too great for absolution. The Bible acknowledges David flaws but honors him for his devotion to God. This raises the question of why God called him a man after my own heart, Acts. Many prefer avoiding consequences to seeking forgiveness. While God forgave David, He did not shield him from the consequences of his actions. Unlike others, David sinned significantly but learnt from his mistakes; he experienced the joy of forgiveness while enduring the consequences of his sins. Many fail to learn from their errors or the resulting consequences. Do you feel beyond redemption due to a grave mistake? Rest assured that God can forgive any transgression upon confession. However, while God forgives us, He may not remove the natural consequences of our actions David life was forever changed by his deeds. As a prophet, Nathan confronted David sins his affair with Bathsheba and Uriah murder with courage and skill. Would you seek divine intervention for a fresh start? The Bible states, If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land. This assurance from God indicates that if we are amenable and compliant, Christ will forgive and erase even our most stubborn blemishes. God is an unconditional forgiver, and through Christ death, our Heavenly Father is prepared to forgive anyone for anything. This means that anyone who seeks His forgiveness will receive it, and all sins repented and confessed will be pardoned through Christ shed blood.

title: Test #118: Legal Matter - Appeal Against Bombay High Court
text: The foundation for this reference relating to the interpretation of Section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 to a Bench of seven judges has its origins in three decisions of this Court. While hearing the appeal against the decision of the Bombay High Court, a Bench of three learned Judges expressed the view that the content, scope and what constitutes a corrupt practice under sub- sections 3 of Section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 needs to be clearly and authoritatively laid down to avoid a miscarriage of justice in interpreting corrupt practice. The Bench was of opinion that the appeal requires be hearing and deciding by a larger Bench of five Judges of this Court on three specific questions of law. In appeal before this Court, the Constitution Bench noticed an anomalous situation arising out of an amendment to Section 123 of the Act in 1961 inasmuch as it appeared that a corrupt practice for the purposes of the Act prior to the amendment could cease to be a corrupt practice after the amendment. On the one hand the deletion of certain words from the sub-section widened the scope of the sub-section while the addition of a word seemingly had the opposite effect. Since there are certain other significant observations made in the order passed by the Constitution Bench, it would be more appropriate to quote the relevant text of the Order. Thereafter, when Abhiram Singh was taken up for consideration by the Constitution Bench, an order was made that since one of the questions involved in the present appeal is already referred to a larger Bench of seven Judges, we think it appropriate to refer this appeal to a limited extent regarding interpretation of sub-section 3 of Section 123 of the 1951 Act to a larger Bench of seven Judges. It is under these circumstances that these appeals are before us on a limited question of the interpretation of sub-section 3 of Section 123 of the Act. In this case, the Constitution Bench held that an appeal to the electorate on a ground personal to the candidate relating to his language attracts the prohibition of a corrupt practice under Section 100 read with Section 123 of the Act. The Constitution Bench made a reference to sub-section 3 of Section 123 of the Act in rather broad terms. The Constitution Bench read into Section 123 of the Act the concept of a secular democracy and the purity of elections which must be free of unhealthy practices. It is quite clear from a reading of the above passages that the concern of Parliament in enacting Section 123 of the Act was to provide a check on the undesirable development of appeals to religion, race, caste, community or language of any candidate. Therefore, to maintain the sanctity of the democratic process and to avoid vitiating the secular atmosphere of democratic life, an appeal to any of the factors would void the election of the candidate committing the corrupt practice?

title: Test #119: Politicians Asking for More Children
text:
Yet again some politicians are asking women to have more children. Chandrababu Naidu is telling Andhraites that it is their responsibility to have more children, not for themselves but for the nation. Stalin is telling Tamilians to rethink the small family as it is likely to decrease Tamil Nadu seats in Parliament. But nowhere in the world do people have children thinking of their nation or legislatures or govt. Do these two CMs imagine that it is political slogans that brought down the country total fertility rate from 4.6 in 1980 to 1.91 in 2021? No slogan, from no political dispensation, can railroad this into existence. India experience with heavy-handed govt interventions shows how counterproductive they can be, while China shows what terrible side-effects they can have. Sanjay Gandhi slogan, Hum Do Hamare Do, didnot makes Indians have fewer kids. What did was that, over decades, there has been imperfect but still substantive work on school expansion and healthcare provision, including contraception options, alongside wider availability of economic opportunities. Hence, the great change in what people want from their lives and their children lives. The same true for girl child education. Slogans would not do the trick. Targeted fiscal incentives aimed at social groups that see girl children as burden will possibly change minds. Society is an incredibly complicated system; tweaking it to a govt desire is a fantasy. But its a fantasy fervently believed by politicians, in the West or the East, in democracies or dictatorships. Just how complex it gets is clear from this case: Bengal has a low fertility rate, high school enrolment for girls, large schemes for their welfare but also a disturbingly high child marriage rate. This paradox has no obvious policy explanation. Earlier this year, Stalin was celebrating how Tamil Nadu accounts for over 40% of the entire female workforce across India manufacturing sector. That has a lot to do with women in the state having fewer children. There can be no walk back on reproductive autonomy. Indeed, there are too many women who are still waiting in the wings to earn that freedom. As Nobel Laureate economist Claudia Goldin highlighted, having both family and career is still way harder for women than men. Make this easier for women, and they may have more kids. Make slogans, you will be ignored rightly. As one takes to spiritual inquiry, the focus shifts from the external God to our deepest core within, to our real Identity.

title: Test #120: To Seek Ultimate Truth, Start With No-Belief
text:
There is a widespread misunderstanding that spiritual study and practice are mystic and other-worldly and necessary only at the end of life. But the purpose of spirituality is to enable us to grow with the right knowledge about ourselves and the world and to live with freedom and fulfillment. The goal of spirituality is to make us masters of the world by enabling us to overcome our own minds and intelligence. Right from birth, we become slaves to objects and circumstances. Spirituality redeems us from this slavery and enables us to embrace any situation with equanimity. It is wrong to consider spiritual practices as religious in the conventional sense. Hinduism is neither a religion. It represents the thoughts and experiences, discoveries and conclusions of a civilisation quest for the ultimate goal of human life and society. The core of Hinduism is its eternal spiritual wisdom enshrined in the Upanishads, which are truly the record of experimental discoveries made by our rishis, who researched the ultimate Reality and discovered our real Identity. Just like the knowledge of Physics, Chemistry, or Mathematics is not dependent on whether you are an American, African or Indian, whether you are a Hindu, Christian or Atheist, the knowledge of one real Identity, as revealed in the Upanishads, is also independent of one racial, ethnic, and religious identity. That is why spirituality begins where religion concludes. A God-believing person is a believer in his concept of God. An atheist is also a believer but in the concept of No-God. Both of them are believers they believe in some concept of their mind. This a priori belief stifles their inquiry. A seeker of ultimate Truth should start with no belief. Why do we look for a creator? Because we find that everything in the world follows causality. The causality we see all around us makes us think there must be a cause for the objective universe. But, the same rationality, which compels us to look for a cause behind everything, tells us that the very nature of causality is a never-ending chain, and the ultimate Reality, by definition, must be beyond causality. Causality works within the ken of duality, but the ultimate Reality must transcend duality. In other words, there cannot be any objective cause behind the objective universe. Then, how do we proceed to find the ultimate Reality? Is there any truth that transcends objectude? Look within to discover the transcendental non-dual Self, on which appears the entire objectude as well as subjectude.

title: Test #122: Legal Matter - Instant Writ Petition Filed
text: The instant writ petition has been filed by two petitioners, Transparency International India and Centre for Media Studies. The cause for the petitioners, to approach this Court, seems to emerge from a study, described as India Corruption Study to improve Governance, conducted by Centre for Media Study, and published by Transparency International India. It was sought to be repeatedly highlighted, that the above research program taken on hand by Centre for Media Studies, was a general study on governance, predominantly with reference to the bureaucracy, and the functioning of the administrative machinery. Yet it was acknowledged, that there were references to the functioning of the judiciary, as well. Even though, the above study was conducted independently, with reference to each State, yet the relevant study, which has brought the petitioners of the instant writ petition to this Court, pertains to the State of Jammu and Kashmir, and is limited to the findings recorded therein, with reference only to the lower judiciary. The compilation of the views of those who were asked to express their views led to the inference, that 92% of the lower judiciary in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, was perceived to be corrupt. A perusal of the order, according to the learned counsel for the respondent, makes it abundantly clear, that the same is in the nature of a show cause notice, calling for the explanation of the notices. This position, in our view, merits acceptance. It is also relevant to mention, that the order also brought out, that the same was being passed under the provisions of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1997. It is in the above perspective, that we will examine the submissions of the rival counsel, while adjudicating upon the controversy in hand. Thereafter it was pointed out on behalf of the petitioners, that further notices were also issued, for the same purpose. The notice categorically expressed, now again you are being issued notice to cause your appearance or through your authorized representative to answer all material questions as to why cognizance as taken above be not proceeded against you on or before next date of hearing. It is therefore apparent, that the personal presence of the petitioners or others, to whom the above notices were issued, was not sought. The pleadings in the instant writ petition, more particularly paragraph thereof, acknowledge that, Transparency International India received the show cause notice, and Centre for Media Studies received the same. Having received the aforesaid notices, the following response was addressed by the Centre for Media Studies, to the Judicial Magistrate, Jammu & Kashmir. It is necessary to notice, that the petitioners informed the Judicial Magistrate that while it was open to the Magistrate to make a reference to the High Court, under the Contempt of Courts Act, the Magistrate had no right to suo moto initiate proceedings, under the Contempt of Courts Act. title: Test #123: Two Belts and Fractured Country
text:
In the waning days of the US presidential election, Republican nominee Trump will be holding rallies in New York and California. And while these are the most populous states in the country, the announcement of these rallies has been met with disbelief from political observers, because in US, its not the states with the biggest population that matter. A small group of swing states decides the election. The US presidential election is not really one election, but 51 separate elections, one for each of the states and the capital district. Each of these elections has its own rules: for instance, in some states, the election is done entirely by mail, in some; voters are required to show ID in order to cast a ballot. What nearly all these elections have in common, though, is that they’re winner-take-all elections, in which the candidate who gets the most votes in the state gets that state’s delegates in the Electoral College, the antiquated body that actually decides who wins the election. That winner-take-all process means that candidates for president only pay attention to a few states, comprising a small portion of US. If a state is solidly Democratic like New York, or California there no reason for anyone to campaign there. Any time or effort Republicans put into those states during a presidential election would be wasted, as there no way they can win it, and Democrats dont bother either, as they know they will win anyway. The same holds true for big Republican states, like Texas. So it makes sense for both candidates to put all of their time, money and effort into just those states called swing states that could favour either candidate. And that exactly what they do. The seven swing states that will decide this year election are home to only about in 6 Americans, but voters there are being bombarded with TV ads, people knocking on their doors, calls and postcards from volunteers across the country urging them to vote. In the city of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania alone, the two major parties are projected to spend around TV ads in the last two months of the election. Across the river from Philadelphia, in solidly Democratic New Jersey, one of the populous US states, the candidates will spend basically nothing. If Trump fans in New Jersey want to put up a yard sign supporting him, they will likely have to pay for it. Exactly which states are swing states varies over time. Twenty years ago, Ohio and Florida were the most important, but both are solidly Republican now. The states that are expected to push this election towards one candidate or the other in 2024 can be divided into two groups: the rust belt and the Sun Belt.

title: Test #124: India Reverts to 2020 LAC Patrolling Terms
text:
After long negotiations, India and China have finally agreed to return to the patrolling arrangements along the LAC in eastern Ladakh that were in place before the Galwan clashes in 2020. The agreement covers the areas of Depsang and Demchok. External affairs minister S Jaishankar had recently said that about 75% of disengagement problems with China had been sorted out and that the key issue was the increasing militarisation of the frontier. Now, those negotiations are going on. We made some progress. We still have some things to do, he had said. Following the foreign ministry announcement, EAM Jaishankar said the two countries had gone back to where the situation was in 2020. We can say that the disengagement process with China has been completed. There are areas which for various reasons after 2020 because they had blocked us so we had blocked them. So what has happened is we have reached an understanding, which will allow the patrolling, he said. There was no specific mention of the withdrawal of tens of thousands of additional troops stationed by the two countries along the border in Ladakh and there was neither any statement from Beijing on the matter. Demchok is close to the southernmost part of the LAC in Ladakh, near the state border with Himachal Pradesh. A village in the region was the site of a Chinese incursion during the 1962 conflict but PLA troops did not venture beyond. It was the first place where China prevented Indian authorities from building civic infrastructure, including a road. Depsang Plains is a flat area near Daulat Beg Oldie in the northwest portion of the disputed Aksai Chin region in UT Ladakh. The disputed area had been occupied by China until India began making headway into the region and now has a road leading to it. Because of the flat terrain, it allows for easy movement of troops and vehicles, including tanks. Foreign secretary Vikram Misri said on Monday the agreement was thrashed out by Indian and Chinese negotiators after weeks of talks aimed at resolving the issues that arose after the Chinese military action in eastern Ladakh in 2020. Indian and Chinese troops first clashed on May 5, 2020, on the north bank of the Pangong Tso lake. There was a major clash on the night of June 15 between an Indian patrol and PLA troops in Galwan Valley with casualties on both sides. Amid claims and counter-claims regarding the capture of Indian territory in May and June 2020, there were satellite images showing China constructing bunkers and trenches and setting up tents along Pangong Tso lake. It even reportedly built a pier on the lake for boats. After the 2020 clashes, China aggressively built up its presence along the LAC in Ladakh, including by bringing in troops and armoured vehicles.

title: Test #125: Bhartiya Nyay Sanhita, 2023 - 1
text: The Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860 is the principal law on criminal offences in India.  Offences covered include those affecting: human body such as assault and murder, property such as extortion and theft, public order such as unlawful assembly and rioting, public health, safety, decency, morality, and religion, defamation, and offences against the state. Over the years, the IPC has been amended to add new offences, amend existing ones and change the quantum of punishment. Courts have also de-criminalised certain offences such as consensual intercourse between same-sex adults, adultery and attempt to commit suicide. Several states have also amended the IPC to provide different punishments for sexual offences, selling minors for prostitution, adulteration of food and drugs and sacrilege of religious texts. Several Law Commission reports have recommended amendments to the IPC on subjects including offences against women, food adulteration, and death penalty. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaces the IPC. It largely retains the provisions of the IPC, adds some new offences, removes offences that have been struck down by courts, and increases penalties for several offences. It was examined by the Standing Committee on Home Affairs. The IPC criminalises acts such as murder, abetment of suicide, assault and causing grievous hurt. The BNS retains these provisions. It adds new offences such as organised crime, terrorism, and murder or grievous hurt by a group on certain grounds. The IPC criminalises acts such as rape, voyeurism, stalking and insulting the modesty of a woman. The BNS retains these provisions. It increases the threshold for the victim to be classified as a major, in the case of gangrape, from 16 to 18 years of age. It also criminalises sexual intercourse with a woman by deceitful means or making false promises. The BNS removes the offence of sedition. It instead penalises the following: exciting or attempting to excite secession, armed rebellion, or subversive activities, encouraging feelings of separatist activities, or endangering the sovereignty or unity and integrity of India. These offences may involve exchange of words or signs, electronic communication, or use of financial means. The BNS defines terrorism as an act that intends to: threaten the unity, integrity, and security of the country, intimidate the general public, or disturb public order. Punishment for attempting or committing terrorism includes: death or life imprisonment and a fine of Rs 10 lakh, if it results in death of a person, or imprisonment between five years and life, and a fine of at least five lakh rupees. Organised crime includes offences such as kidnapping, extortion, contract killing, land grabbing, financial scams, and cybercrime carried out on behalf of a crime syndicate. Attempting or committing organised crime will be punishable with: death or life imprisonment and a fine of Rs 10 lakh, if it results in death of a person, or imprisonment between five years and life, and a fine of at least five lakh rupees. The BNS adds murder or grievous hurt by five or more people on specified grounds, as an offence. These grounds include race, caste, sex, language, or personal belief. The punishment for such murder is a minimum of seven years imprisonment to life imprisonment or death. The BNS conforms to some decisions of the Supreme Court. These include omitting adultery as an offence and adding life imprisonment as one of the penalties (in addition to the death penalty) for murder or attempt to murder by a life convict.

title: Test #127: Super Human Large Language Models
text:
The very term machine intelligence is premised on the limits of human potential since machines are created by human beings. If machines could think for themselves, without having to be pre-programmed by humans, one can safely assume that artificial intelligence is coming of age that there is the possibility of their having common sense, to make decisions outside of their packaged abilities. But then, large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and other such generative AI platforms have not so far evidenced independent, volitional thought processes or actions. They are as yet mere tools, functioning as per human design patterns and inputs. It follows therefore that for truly creative writers, pre-programmed AI tools like ChatGPT are hindrances rather than enablers as they cramp imagination, limiting the writer infinite creativity. If and when the day comes when machines can think for themselves independent of human inputs, only then can we conclude that yes, we have a huge threat or wonderful ally on our hands, depending on the perspective from which you view LLMs, for instance. And depending on the extent to which you can exercise some sort of control so that AI does not go off the rails. It will also open up the debate as to whether machines can have consciousness, for, to be self-aware and ruminate on the nature of the higher Self, so far, one need to be human with the ability to carry out this kind of thought process. At best, generative AI could serve the purpose of guidebooks that students resort to on the eve of examinations, with all the risks of rote learning, and inbuilt errors. Autocorrect, a boon for quick reviews and proof-reading, can also completely change the context and meaning of a sentence or phrase when spell checks are done without common sense. This is how causal is corrected to casual and Hare Krishn becomes Hate Krishn! Hence relying on generative AI completely when it is still functioning on human inputs, even if it has some amount of deductive ability, can be a slippery slope. Can AI be engineered to the extent that it can have its own common sense? In other words, can AI be endowed with the power of discrimination? Can it deal with abstract scenarios? Human cognitive ability, intuition, emotion and imagination are attributes that are currently absent in AI including LLMs. So, AI response is always constrained by facts, figures and cold logic rather than reasoning and common sense. A choreographed, deliberate response or reaction to a situation is not always the optimal way to deal with it; more human qualities like self-awareness, reflection, reasoning, imagination and compassion can play far more crucial roles.

title: Test #128: Indian Elephant's Genetic Diversity
text:
A recent study led by Raman Sukumar of the Indian Institute of Science and Uma Ramakrishnan of the National Centre for Biological Sciences in Bengaluru, has found that India is home to five genetically distinct populations of Asian elephants. These groups are spread across northern, central and southern India. The researchers, who analysed whole genome sequences from captive and wild elephant blood samples, say these findings could guide conservation efforts by pinpointing specific populations in need of customised strategies. Historically, elephants migrated from the north to the south, with each dispersal resulting in a decline in genetic diversity, says Ramakrishnan. The northwest and northeast populations, found in the foothills of the Himalayas, share similarities yet are genetically distinct from other groups in India. The Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers are potential barriers to gene flow in these regions. The researchers add that the elephant population south of the Shencottah Gap in the Western Ghats of Kerala and Tamil Nadu had the lowest variation suggestive of inbreeding, which warranted a more detailed study. There no cause for immediate alarm as there has been cases of populations such as the Bornean elephants which originated from a single-digit source population but have subsequently grown to sizeable numbers without any apparent issues. The shifting of the bull elephant from the Munnar region in Kerala to the Upper Kodhayar region in Tamil Nadu would help with gene flow across the Shencottah Gap. The most likely explanation for these findings is a serial founder effect, where only a few elephants from each original population migrate and establish new ones. These resulting populations tend to be small, which increases the risk of inbreeding depression (where harmful genetic variants are more likely to be inherited from both the parents due to breeding among closely related animals). Located south of the Shencottah Gap, the most recently established population shows the lowest genetic diversity and faces the highest risk of inbreeding depression. There may be fewer than 50 elephants, says Ramakrishnan. This population is at a higher risk of extinction. Sukumar agrees but says there are promising exceptions to as sumptions about low genetic variation and extinction risks. Sabah in Borneo is home to more than 1,000 elephants, a population that survives and multiplies despite a narrow genetic base. The Addo elephants in South Africa have grown from just 11 to more than 600 in a century. We need more studies on elephant genomes for better management strategies. Geographic patterns like these are rare in large mammals such as elephants because their long-range movements usually blur such distinctions.

title: Test #129: Legal Matter - The Special Leave Petition
text:
Mr. Rai submitted that the petitioner was acquitted by the appellate court and the High Court, while disposing of the revision filed against the order of acquittal, exceeded its jurisdiction in passing an order that resulted into the conviction of the petitioner. He submitted that in exercise of the powers under Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, an order of acquittal cannot be converted into an order of conviction and what the High Court could, at best do was to order a retrial of the petitioner. In support of the submission, he relied upon the decisions of this Court in a case of 1998. We find no merit in the submission of Mr. Nagendra Rai and we are satisfied that the decisions relied upon by him have no application to the facts of this case. All that the High Court has done is to set aside the order passed by the appellate court and restore the order of conviction and sentence passed by the trial court. At this stage, it will be useful to take a brief look at the facts and circumstances that led the High Court to interfere in the matter. While the trial was going on, the accused purported to enter into some sort of a settlement with the complainant, his wife. In terms of the settlement, he accepted to take the complainant back at his house even though he had taken a second wife in the meanwhile. Hence, when the complainant was examined before the trial court she did not press the charges but expressed her willingness to live with her husband and his second wife. Later on, however, before the conclusion of the trial she filed a petition before the trial court stating that the accused, the husband, had breached the settlement and thrown her out from his house. In those circumstances, the trial court recalled her for re-examination as a court witness under Section 311 of the Cr.P.C. On her examination as a court witness, she fully supported the allegations made by her in the complaint. Eventually, the trial court convicted the petitioner under Sections 494 and 498-A of the Penal Code. In appeal, the appellate court held that the order passed by the trial court, recalling the complainant for examination as a court witness was bad and invalid and her evidence as a court witness could not be taken into account for recording the finding of guilt against the petitioner.

title: Test #130: Decent, Humble, Humorous - Ratan Tata
text:
Ratan Tata passing leaves a significant void in the Indian business firmament. He possibly saved India largest and most respected business conglomerate from irrelevance and in the process became a role model for a generation of Indian businesses and start-ups. In leading an over century-old enterprise with many lifers, Ratan Tata showed a path-breaking willingness to take risks and back young talent. Scores of Tata managers assigned major responsibilities in their twenties will attest to this, as will many appointed CEOs in their thirties. He didnot mind ruffling feathers, constantly exhorting those around him to question the unquestioned. His response to my concern that this writer lacked an MBA qualification was: All you need to succeed in the corporate world is good common sense. That is pretty much how he conducted his affairs, backing his instincts on people and issues. At well over six feet in height and always immaculately dressed, Tata had an imposing physical presence. But he maintained a fundamental level of decency and humility, urging his office to show empathy when engaging with stakeholders with grievances and claims. We warmed to his ability to laugh loudly, sometimes at himself, and his incredible mimicry of colleagues. Given to doodling during long meetings, he once drew the bald heads of three senior Tata Sons directors to keep himself entertained. Sadly, this sense of humour began to vanish as pressures of office started wearing him down midway through his chairmanship. Senior colleagues retired and were replaced by a younger, more diffident lot who tended to be intimidated by his larger than-life stature. As he neared retirement, business disappointments and corporate scandals such as the so-called 2G scam would cause him considerable pain. Having assumed charge of the Tata Group in 1991, the year India began to liberalise its economy, Tata was forced to focus initially on consolidation. Convinced that individual Tata companies would do better if they were guided by a powerful Group Centre, rather than each trying to operate on its own, he saw off internal opposition from satraps like Russi Mody at Tata Steel and Ajit Kerkar at Indian Hotels. Parallelly, he undertook key initiatives to boost the competitiveness of the group, investing in talent and capabilities at the Group Centre; promoting a culture of quality consciousness via the 1995 launch of JRD Quality Values Award Programme; and securing access to intellectual property to help companies improve their competitiveness, including through joint ventures with global leaders like IBM, Lucent Technologies, Honeywell and AIG.

title: Test #131: Does God Depends on Us for Existence?
text:
This is the unasked question underlying the theme of the 2023 film, Freud Last Session, which recounts a fictional meeting between Freud and the Oxbridge scholar and author, CS Lewis, which takes place in London as the world is engulfed in the doom-laden onset of World War II. Freud, suffering from terminal oral cancer, the unendurable pain of which would compel him to commit suicide a few weeks later, is portrayed as an unshakeable atheist, a conviction enjoined upon him both by his adherence to rationality and science as well as by the happen stance of the tragic loss of his daughter and his five-year-old grandson. What sort of God is this who takes the lives of innocent children? asks Freud of Lewis and of the film audience. Though Lewis and Freud probably never met, separated as they were by a generation, the founder of psychoanalysis would have demanded to know why Lewis, who had long been an avowed atheist, would suddenly convert to devout Christianity. The film is based on a book by American academic, Armand Nicholi, titled The Question of God, which hinges on that anguished query: What monstrous Deity wilfully claims the lives of children? Is what we call religion nothing more than escapist wish fulfilment? God a magnified father figure, a personification of authority to make us pliant subjects of church and state? Like the book on which it is based, the film does not take sides for or against the two diametrically opposed views, that of the staunch atheist and that of the equally fervent believer. But the debate itself evokes the concept of theodicy that Lewis went on to explore in his own book, The Problem of Pain, which deals with that most perplexing and haunting of questions: Why do bad things happen to good people? The term theodicy, derived from the Greek theo for God and dike for justice, was coined by the eighteenth-century German philosopher Leibniz and is an attempt to justify why an omnipotent creator can condone the existence of evil, can permit the slaughter of innocents, in his creation. What sort of cosmic CEO is God, anyway? There are as many takes on theodicy as there are theologians, but that of CS Lewis in The Problem of Pain is both compelling and provocative, rising as it does another bogey of philosophical and theological speculation, which is that of free will. Lewis argued that an omnipotent God could work miracles and intercede to avert suffering, but this would deny humankind the capacity of free will.

title: Test #132: Uttrakhand Set to Bring in UCC on Nov 9
text:
The nine-member panel for drafting the rules and regulations for the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) after its final meeting Monday said that the process has been completed and the draft is being sent for printing. The panel headed by ex-chief secretary Shatrughan Singh and formed in Feb this year would subsequently hand over the report to chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami, paving the way for the implementation of UCC in Uttarakhand likely on Nov 9 the state foundation day. Once implemented, Uttarakhand would become the first state in the country after Independence to have such a law. Confirming the development, Singh, the panel head, said, After several rounds of meetings, we have been successful in finalising the rules and regulations. Once we get the printed version, we will take an appointment from the CM and hand over the report to him. In accordance with the CM announcement regarding implementation of UCC on Nov 9, we have completed our report on time. Once the report is handed over, the state govt will take further steps. Monday meeting, regarded by many as an extremely crucial one, held at Bijapur Guest House in the state capital, discussed some key finer points related to registration of marriage, divorce, live-in, birth and death certificate or will in the Himalayan state. Panel member Manu Gaur told: A major highlight is that the panel has ensured that people do not need to rush to govt offices to get the registration work done. It can be done online with a few simple clicks. We have developed a web portal and a mobile application, which is integrated with several portals of the Union govt. He added: For people who are not tech savvy, we have provided an option of getting themselves registered via the 15,000 common service centers across the state. A six-month time period has also been given to people to register their marriages. The process is a simple one. Those who have their marriage registered in other states will also be required to upload their registration number and other details, Gaur said, adding that those not registering their marriage would not be provided benefits of government schemes. title: Test #133: Master Artisans Fight to Move the Needle
text:
The free market is a beast that will not be shackled. Its the reason the bottle of Worcestershire sauce in someone fridge is probably from Nagpur, your neighbour precious Persian rug was woven in Agra Old Vijay Nagar, and Assam gamosa used to be Surat money-spinning business. In J&K, master artisans Mehrajud-din Beigh and Noorullah have been fighting to save the centuries-old Kashmiri art of chain-stitch embroidery, Kashida, from the ravages of factory production at scale since long before GI tagging entered the protectionist discourse. My scariest thought is that kashidakari will vanish. You will still buy rugs with complex, traditional Kashida patterns, but they will all be machine woven. That is doing injustice to this great art form, bemoans Beigh, 65. Kashida embroidery dates back to the 15th century, flourishing under the patronage of Zain-ul-Abidin of the Shah Mir dynasty that presided over the Kashmir sultanate. The primary tool artisans skilled in kashidakari use is a hooked needle called an aari. The process starts with sketching the design on the chosen fabric and then filling it with chain stitches using fine silk or wool threads. The design is a raised, textured surface that is visually intricate, creates a riot of colours, and is soft to the touch. The inexhaustible display of colours, variegated birds, luscious fruits, majestic mountains, shimmering lakes – all find a place in Kashmir embroidery, she wrote. Blogger Mala Chandrashekhar, who writes extensively on art and culture, points out that artisans often use subtle colour variations within a single motif to create depth and dimension. Each motif and pattern holds significance. Chinar leaves symbolise the valley beauty, almond blossoms denote hope and renewal, and paisley represents fertility and abundance. Beigh, a resident of Srinagar Chanpora, started learning the art of Kashida from an artisan in his neighbourhood when he was seven. For someone who spent over five decades as a practitioner of kashidakari, he still makes only about Rs 2,000 a month for three to four pieces. While Beigh son chose to be a salesperson rather than carry forward his father legacy, the senior artisan remains eager to help keep the art form alive. If the govt assists, I will happily mentor whoever from the next generation is willing to learn. Noorullah, from Khwaja Bazar, is from a family of Kashida artisans, but his children two daughters and a son arenot keen on continuing the tradition. They are studying and would rather do something else. I donot blame them, he says.

title: Test #135: UPI users are Worse Hit as Online Payment Fraud
text:
Digital payments, internet banking victimisation and fraud calls has surged in the city. The data shared by Delhi Police revealed that until June this year, 25,924 UPI-related complaints, 5,312 internet banking complaints and 5,486 fraud calls or vishing complaints were filed on the National Cyber Crime Portal (NCRP). A police officer said UPI-related frauds assumed different methods, one common tactic being sending victims fake scanner images and requesting them to pay money. There are several cases where scammers made phone calls to people and first sent them edited images of a UPI transaction that they had supposedly sent to the victim by mistake. They would then send a fake scanner image and ask the victim to send the money back, the officer said. These scammers also threaten the victim with a police complaint if the money wasnot returned. Due to fear, the victims often transferred the amount to them. Another officer revealed that fraudsters often employed known as friend or relative impersonation. The scammers contact their targets posing as a close relative or friend living abroad and claiming to be in financial straits due to a medical emergency or apressing legal. They urgently request a substantial sum of money. The fraudsters may employ various tactics to create a sense of urgency and manipulate their victims into believing the false narrative, the officer said. Unsuspecting victims, believing the claims, transfer the requested funds without a thorough inquiry. In net banking fraud, victims receive malicious emails that gain control of their device and net banking account. Sometimes, the scammers resort to deceptive tactics like sending out emails that seem to originate at reputable financial organisations, the officer explained. The messages contain requests for private details, including usernames, passwords and account numbers, all under false pretences. Some recipients unknowingly provide the fraudsters access to their accounts and financial resources. Frauds also employ a deceptive tactic known as voice phishing, especially when targeting older adults. The cons pose as legitimate bank representatives, often using sophisticated techniques to mimic the voice and mannerisms of a real bank executive. The goal is to manipulate the victims into clicking on malicious links or attachments or divulging confidential details about their bank accounts. This information can then be used to steal funds or commit identity theft. Unscrupulous operators also contact people, assuring them they have won a prize from a bank, ranging from a travel voucher to an additional debit or credit card.
